Candidi, i.e., A. neotritici, A. pragensis, A. taichungensis, A. tenebricus and A. subalbidus have shorter stipes than A. campestris. Micromorphology: Conidiophores 500–1000 × 5–10 (–20) µm. Conidial heads variable in size, globose to ra- diate, 200–500 µm in diameter. Conidiophores smooth, vesicles globose to subglobose, 10–40 µm, metulae wedge shaped 5–8 × 2.5–3.5 µm to 25–30 × 10–12 µm. Phialides cylindrical with a short distinct neck, 5–8 × 2–2.5(–3) µm. Conidia colourless, globose, 3.0–3.5(–4) µm, smooth-walled.
Diagnosis: Aspergillus candidus is sister to A. dobrogensis and closely related to A. campestris and A. magnus. In general, A. candidus has smaller vesicles, shorter and narrower stipes and also shorter phialides and metulae compared to A. dobrogensis (Table 5). Aspergillus dobrogensis colonies also have a larger diameter than A. candidus on MEA, CYA and CY20S (Table 4). However, most of these differences can be interpreted as a trend across the whole species, while some isolates show identical dimensions to A. dobrogensis strains (Fig. 7). Thus, distinguishing between them can be problematic in practice. Aspergillus magnus colonies have a smaller diameter and it has wider and longer stipes, vesicles and metulae than A. candidus. Aspergillus campestris has usually bright yellow colonies and produces stipes, vesicles and metulae which are longer/wider than in A. candidus. Aspergillus pragensis grows more restricted on all media while A. neotritici, A. tenebricus and A. taichungensis colonies have a larger diameter on MEA, CYA and CY20S. The latter three species grow at 35 °C or higher temperatures (Table 6). Aspergillus taichungensis and A. tenebricus produce shorter stipes and A. tenebricus has longer phialides and metulae compared to A. candidus.
Similar species: Aspergillus candidus is related to A. tritici. The latter can grow at 37 °C, while the former cannot. Aspergillus dobrogensis differs from A. candidus by its longer and broader stipes and smaller vesicles. Almost all isolates of A. dobrogensis produce sclerotia on MEA and CYA, while the majority of A. candidus strains did not produce sclerotia on CYA and none of the isolates produced them on MEA. Macromorphology: Colonies growing slowly on CYA at 25 °C (diameter 13–20 mm after 7 days), usually thin with some aerial mycelium, intermixed with conidiophores arising from the agar or from the aerial mycelium. Conidial heads white, later cream, in fresh isolates often wet. The colony reverse is uncoloured to pale yellow. Colony diameter on MEA 8–14 mm and on YES 19–33 mm after 7 days, colony reverse cream yellow. On CREA poor growth and no acid production.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Chemical markers: Aspergillazine A, chloroflavonins, dechlorochlorflavonin, 3-hydroxyterphenyllin, terphe- nyllin and the related candidusin A & B and terprenins, xanthoascins. Odour weak.
Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus candidus is common world-wide. It occurs on corn, wheat and other cereals and has also been found in peanuts and on other foods and in soil. Aspergillus tritici is also common in cereals and can cause active heating. Both are good lipase producers.
Physiology: Aspergillus candidus is halo-tolerant. It can tolerate low pH values and rather low water activities.
Biotechnological applications: Several “A. candidus” used in biotechnology proved to be white mutants of A. flavus or A. oryzae.
Biodeterioration and pathology: May deteriorate ce- reals.

Culture characteristics: Culture characteristics (at 25 °C after 2 wk): Colonies on MEA white (3A1) with a tint of yellowish white (4A2), flat, texture granular to floccose, sporulation abundant, margins entire, exudate absent, reverse light yellow (4A4) or pale yellow (4A3). Colonies on CYA white (3A1) with a tint of yellowish white (4A2) or orange white (5A2), flat or slightly centrally raised, texture granular to floccose, sporulation abundant, margins entire or slightly undulate, exudate absent, reverse light yellow (4A5) or brownish orange (5C3). Colonies on CZA white (3A1) to pale yellow (1A3, 3A3), flat, texture waxy to granular, sporulation weak, margins entire or irregular, exudate absent, reverse pale yellow (3A3) or light yellow (4A4). Colonies on CY20S white (3A1), flat or slightly centrally raised, texture floccose, granular or velvety, radially or irregularly folded, sporulation abundant, margins entire to diffuse or slightly erose, exudate absent, reverse light yellow (4A4, 4A5). Soluble pigment production after 4 wk was examined in nine strains: five of them (CCF 488, CCF 5172, CCF 6200, CCF 3996, NRRL 58959) were able to produce it and four (CBS 566.65T, CCF 4659, CCF 4713, CCF 6195) not. Dark brown to black soluble pigment (3−4 mm around colonies) was observed on CZA in strains CCF 488 and CCF 6200. Brown soluble pigment was observed on CZA in strains CCF 5172 and CCF 3996 (2−4 mm around colonies) and on CYA in strain CCF 3996. Brownish yellow soluble pigment was observed on CZA in strain NRRL 58959. No soluble pigment was observed on MEA and CY20S in any strain. Sclerotia production after 4 wk was examined in nine strains. Five of them (CCF 488, CCF 5172, CCF 6200, CCF 3996, NRRL 58959) were able to produce sclerotia, while no sclerotia were observed in the remaining strains (CBS 566.65T, CCF 4659, CCF 4713, CCF 6195). Brown to black sclerotia covered by mycelium were present on CZA in five mentioned strains. No sclerotia were observed on MEA, CYA and CY20S in any examined strain.
Cardinal temperatures: Cardinal temperatures (on MEA, after 2 wk): Aspergillus candidus is able to grow at 10 °C (8−11 mm), the optimum growth temperature is 25 °C (20−27 mm). The maximum growth temperature is 30 °C (18−25 mm). No growth at 35 °C.
Neotype: Neotype (designated by Samson & Gams 1985): CBS 566.65. Culture ex-type: CBS 566.65 = NRRL 303 = IMI 091889 = ATCC 1002 = IBT 28566 = CCF 5594.
Ecology: Ecology (only records verified by DNA sequencing): The species is known from indoor environments (air, dust), caves, soil, dung, clinical samples, food, metal duct, tunnels of bark beetles, the red flour beetle (Tribolium castaneum) and egg-mass of Arctoscopus japonicus. Aspergillus candidus has been isolated in Canada, Czech Republic, Italy, the Netherlands, Romania, South Korea, Spain and the USA (Fig. 12, Table 1, Supplementary Table S3).

Biodeterioration and pathology: Black rot of grapes (together with A. niger).

Macromorphology: Colonies growing quite fast on CYA at 25 °C (diameter 28–45 mm after 7 days), mostly consisting of a dense felt of blue-green conidial heads. The colony reverse is uncoloured to light brown. Colonies on MEA show similar growth, conidiophores less abundant than on CYA (diameter 25–44 mm after 7 days) and on YES diameter 29–45 mm after 7 days, reverse cream yellow. Colonies on CYA at 37 °C are 9–26 mm in diameter. On CREA good growth and usually moderate to strong acid production.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph can be induced on OA incubated between 25 and 30 °C, neocarpenteles-type (hard, sclerotioid, fawn coloured), heterothallic.

Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus clavatus is common world-wide. It occurs on malting barley, decaying vegetation, soil and dung.
Physiology: Aspergillus clavatus is alkali-tolerant, and it can tolerate low and high pH values and rather low water activities.
Biotechnological applications: Aspergillus clavatus has been used for production of sarcins, bioactive proteins.
Biodeterioration and pathology: May deteriorate malting barley.

Diagnosis: See section “Diagnosis” of A. candidus for more details. Aspergillus dobrogensis differs from A. candidus, A. pragensis, A. taichungensis, A. tenebricus and A. subalbidus by its longer and broader stipes and larger vesicles (Table 5, Fig. 6). Aspergillus campestris can be differentiated by its yellow colonies. Aspergillus dobrogensis colonies have a larger diameter than A. campestris, A. candidus, A. pragensis, A. magnus and A. subalbidus on MEA, CYA and CY20S, while A. neotritici and A. taichungensis colonies have a larger diameter than A. dobrogensis on these media (Table 4). Aspergillus subalbidus, A. taichungensis, A. tenebricus and A. neotritici can be differentiated by their ability to grow at 35 °C or even higher temperatures (Table 6).
Culture characteristics: Culture characteristics (at 25 °C after 2 wk): Colonies on MEA white (4A1), sometimes with a tint of yellowish white (4A2), flat or slightly centrally raised, texture floccose, downy or granular, sporulation abundant, margins entire to slightly erose, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse pale yellow (4A3) or light yellow (4A4). Colonies on CYA white (4A1), sometimes with a tint of yellowish white (4A2), flat, centrally raised or umbonate, texture floccose, downy or granular, sporulation abundant, margins entire, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse light yellow (4A4, 4A5). Colonies on CZA white (3A1) to yellowish white (3A2, 4A2), flat, texture waxy to granular, sporulation weak and located in a small area in the colony, margins entire or irregular, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse yellowish white (4A2, 3A2) or pale yellow (3A3, 4A3). Colonies on CY20S white (3A1), flat, centrally raised or umbonate, texture floccose, granular or downy, velvety margins in some strains, sporulation abundant, margins entire, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse light yellow (4A4, 4A5). Sclerotia production after 4 wk was examined in 10 strains, two of them (CCF 4651T, CCF 5570) were able to produce sclerotia and eight of them (CCF 5567, CCF 5568, CCF 4650, CCF 5844, IBT 29476, CCF 5575, CCF 5569 and CCF 5572) not. They were produced superficially, less commonly covered by felt of mycelium. Strain CCF 4651T was able to produce sclerotia on all four media; dark brown sclerotia on MEA, CZA and CY20S and brown sclerotia on CYA. Dark brown sclerotia covered by felt of mycelium were present on CZA in CCF 5570. No sclerotia were observed on MEA, CYA and CY20S in remaining examined strains.
Cardinal temperatures: Cardinal temperatures (on MEA, after 2 wk): Aspergillus dobrogensis is able to grow at 10 °C (9–13 mm) and the optimum growth temperature is 25 °C (23–32 mm). The maximum growth temperature is 30 °C (17–24 mm). No growth at 35 °C.
Ecology: Ecology (only records verified by DNA sequencing): The species is known from caves (bat droppings and guano, sediment, air), indoor environments (air, dust, carpet), mouse dung, herbivore dung and clinical material. It has been isolated in the Czech Republic, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Romania, Spain and the USA (Fig. 12, Table 1). Glässnerová et al.

Species description: Aspergillus fischeri Wehmer
Micromorphology: Ascomata single or borne in small clusters within loose white-creamish hyphae, globose, 80–150(–400) µm in diam, with a 2–3 layers thick wall of flattened cells. Asci 8-spored, globose to somewhat flattened, 8–10 × 10–12 µm. Ascospores biconvex, colourless, 6–7 × 4 µm (including crests), with two equatorial crests and irregular surface ridges. Conidial heads in olive-grey shades, columnar, uniseriate, 100– 150 µm diam. Conidiophores hyaline or slightly coloured, 300–500 µm tall and 4–7 µm diam, smooth-walled. Conidiophore vesicles more or less elongated, 12–18 µm in diam, particularly in the upper part, smooth walled, 100–500 × 5–8 µm. Phialides with a short neck, 6–7 × 2–2.5 µm. Conidia colourless, (sub)globose to ellipsoidal, with slightly roughened walls, 2–2.5 µm in diam or up to 3 µm when globose. The fungus is homothallic.
Similar species: Aspergillus neoglaber (CBS 111.55; CaM: EU014120), A. spinosus (CBS 483.65; CaM: EF669914)
Macromorphology: Colonies growing fast on CYA at 25 °C (diam. 45–68 mm after 7 days), consisting of a dense felt mycelium intermixed with ascomata and aerial hyphae bearing conidiophores. Conidial heads typically columnar. Reverse mostly in shades of cream yellow, and in some strains dark green. Diameter on MEA 66–80 mm after 7 days, colonies white to creamish, granular appea- rance caused by a continuous layer of ascomata; reverse creamish or slightly pinkish. On CREA, poor growth and no acid production.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph known, neosartorya-type, homothallic.
Chemical markers: Aszonalenins, fischerins, fumitre- morgins, fumagillins, helvolic acids, neosartorin, trypa- cidin, tryptoquivalines.
Important mycotoxins: Fumitremorgin A, B & C, ver- ruculogen.
Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus fischeri is quite common world-wide and isolated from soil, rice, cotton, potatoes, groundnuts, leather, paper products. Aspergillus section Fumigati strains with ascospores are heat resistant and cause spoilage in pasteurized products, such as fruit and fruit juices, and yoghurts.
Physiology: Aspergillus fischeri is thermotolerant. Minimum temperature 11–13 °C, optimum 26–45 °C and maximum 51–52 °C. At 24 °C the ascigerous state is predominant, while the conidial state is predominant at 37 °C. The ascospores are heat-resistant, but less than those of A. glaber and A. spinosus.
Biotechnological applications: Aspergillus fischeri strains produce fiscalins, which effectively inhibit the binding of substance P to the human neurokinin receptor.
Biodeterioration and pathology: Sometimes patho- genic to animals and man, but A. fumigatus, A. thermomu- tatus (formerly Neosartorya pseudofischeri) (CBS 208.92; CaM: EF669874) and A. lentulus (CBS 117885; CaM: EF669895) are more common as causes of mycoses.

Micromorphology: Ascomata single or borne in small clusters within loose white-creamish hyphae, globose, 100–250 µm in diam, with a multi-layered cell wall. Similar species: The ascospores of A. hiratsukae resemble those of A. fischeri, but the ascospore surface ornamentation of A. hiratsukae is more finely reticulate due to close-anastomosing ridges. Furthermore, A. hiratsukae grows slower on CYA that A. fischeri. Aspergillus spinosus and A. hiratsukae are related foodborne species and have different ascospores ornamentations. For more details, see A. fischeri.
Macromorphology: Colonies growing slow on CYA at 25 °C (10–20 mm) and faster at 37 °C (25–35 mm) after 7 days, consisting of dense mycelium intermixed with ascomata and aerial hyphae bearing conidiophores. Conidial heads typically columnar; reverse colourless or light brown. Diameter on MEA 25–40 mm after 7 days at 25 °C, colonies white to pale yellow with granular appearance caused by a continuous layer of ascomata. On CREA poor growth and no acid production.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph known, neosartorya-type, homothallic.
Chemical markers: Avenaciolide.
Habitats and distribution: Wordwide, with a preference to (sub)tropic regions. It occurs in pasteurised foods (juices, dairy), soil, cardboard and gypsum board.
Physiology: Thermotolerant; good growth 37 °C. Asper- gillus hiratsukae produces heat resistant ascospores that are able to survive a heat treatment.

Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.

Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus luchuensis is common world-wide. It occurs on grapes, coffee, tea and many other foods.
Physiology: Aspergillus luchuensis is halo-tolerant. It grows well at high temperatures. It can tolerate low pH values and rather low water activities.
Biotechnological applications: Production of nuruk.
Biodeterioration and pathology: Deterioration of grapes.

Species description: Aspergillus magnus Glässnerová & Hubka, sp. nov. MycoBank MB 844202.
Etymology: Latin adj. magnus -a -um, referring to its larger conidiophores (stipe length and width, metulae length and vesicle diameter) compared to related species.
Micromorphology: Conidial heads radiate, biseriate. Diminutive conidiophores usually present. Stipes (excluding diminutive) hyaline, smooth-walled, occasionally finely roughened, non-septate or occasionally septate, (540–)810–1 150(–1 600) × (6–)9–13(–16) μm, vesicles globose to subglobose, (18–)33–39(–45) μm diam, metulae cylindrical or wedge-shaped (V-shaped), (7.5–)9–14(–17) μm long, covering the entire surface of vesicle; phialides ampulliform, (4.5–)5.5–7(–8) μm long. Conidia subglobose to globose, (3–)3.4–3.6(–4) (3.5 ± 0.2 μm) × (2.5–)3.1–3.3(–3.5) (3.2 ± 0.2 μm), occasionally broadly ellipsoidal, smooth-walled, rarely finely roughened.
Typus: Canada, Alberta, Edmonton, mouse collected on horse farm, 1962, J.W. Carmichael (holotype PRM 956934 (dried culture, metabolically inactive), isotypes PRM 956935–956937 (dried culture, metabolically inactive), culture ex-type UAMH 1324 = IBT 14560).
Diagnosis: Aspergillus magnus differs from other section Candidi members by its larger vesicles, longer and wider stipes and longer metulae (Table 5, Fig. 6). Some strains of A. dobrogensis reach similar stipe lengths but they differ from A. magnus by other characters, especially its white colony colour. Aspergillus magnus grows more restricted than other species on all media except for A. pragensis (Table 4). Aspergillus neotritici, A. tenebricus, A. taichungensis and A. subalbidus can be differentiated by their ability to grow at 35 °C or even higher temperatures.
Culture characteristics: Culture characteristics (at 25 °C after 2 wk): Colonies on MEA yellowish grey to pale yellow (3C2–3A3) in the centre, yellowish white (3A2) on the margins, flat, texture floccose, sporulation abundant, margins entire, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse light yellow (4A4). Colonies on CYA pale yellow (3A3) in the centre, yellowish grey (4B2) on the margins, flat, texture floccose, sporulation abundant, margins entire, exudate absent, soluble pigment dark brown (3 mm around colonies after 4 wk), reverse greyish yellow to dark blond (4B4-5D4). Colonies on CZA pale yellow (3A3), flat, texture floccose, sporulation abundant, margins entire, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse pale yellow (3A3). Colonies on CY20S pale yellow (3A3), centrally raised, texture floccose, sporulation abundant, margins entire, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse greyish yellow to dark blond (4B4–5D4). Sclerotia production after 4 wk was not observed on any medium.
Cardinal temperatures: Cardinal temperatures (on MEA, after 2 wk): Aspergillus magnus is able to grow at 10 °C (9–10 mm) and the optimum growth temperature is 25 °C (20–22 mm). The maximum growth temperature is 30 °C (5–7 mm). No growth at 35 °C.
Ecology: Ecology (only records verified by DNA sequencing): The species is known only from a single strain, isolated from a mouse collected on a horse farm in Canada.

Similar species: Aspergillus minisclerotigenes resemble
Macromorphology: Colonies growing fast on CYA at 25 °C and 37 °C (diameter 55–70 mm after 7 days), producing light greyish green conidia. Colony surface velvety on CYA and floccose on oat meal agar and MEA. Sporulation usually quite weak, but there is a dense felt of small sclerotia, diameter 150–300 µm. Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus miniscleroti- genes is pantropically common, and occurs in peanuts, corn, rice and other cereals. This species has often been called A. flavus S type (for the small sclerotia produced).
Physiology: Aspergillus minisclerotigenes is halotolerant. It grows well at high temperatures (even at 42 °C), it can tolerate rather low water activities.
Biodeterioration and pathology: Deteriorate cereals, oilseeds and nuts.

Diagnosis: Aspergillus neotritici colonies have a larger diameter than A. campestris, A. candidus, A. magnus and A. pragensis on all media at 25 °C (Table 4). It grows better than any other species at 30–40 °C and its optimum growth temperature is 30 °C, while in other species, except for A. subalbidus, it is 25 °C (Table 6). It is also the only species which is not able to grow or at least germinate at 10 °C and can grow at 40 °C. Aspergillus pragensis, A. dobrogensis, A. candidus, A. campestris and A. magnus can be differentiated from A. neotritici by their inability to grow at 37 °C. The stipe length and vesicle diameter of A. neotritici is generally longer when compared to A. subalbidus, A. pragensis, A. tenebricus and A. taichungensis (Fig. 7), noting that this omits strains with atypical or uniseriate conidiophores.
Culture characteristics: Culture characteristics (at 25 °C after 2 wk): Colonies on MEA white (3A1) to yellowish white (2A2, 3A2), flat, texture floccose to granular, less commonly velvety (in CCF 4914 and IBT 12659), sporulation abundant, margins entire, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse light yellow (4A4), greyish yellow to golden yellow (4B5–5B7). Colonies on CYA white (3A1) to yellowish white (3A2), flat to centrally raised, usually radially wrinkled, texture floccose, velvety or floccose in CCF 4914 and IBT 12659, margins entire or diffuse, sporulation abundant, exudate usually absent, minute yellow droplets present in CCF 6202, soluble pigment absent, reverse greyish yellow (4B5), reddish yellow (4A6) or brownish orange (5B4) in the centre, light yellow (4A4) on margins. Colonies on CZA white (3A1) to yellowish white (3A2), flat to centrally raised, texture granular, floccose or downy, sporulation abundant, margins entire or irregular, exudate usually absent, minute yellow droplets present in CCF 6202, soluble pigment present in some strains after 4 wk, dark brown soluble pigment (1–2 mm around colonies) present in strains CCF 4030 and CCF 6397, dark green soluble pigment present in strain CCF 4653 (2 mm around colonies), yellow soluble pigment present in strains CCF 3314, CCF 3853T and CCF 4914 (1–5 mm around or between colonies), reverse greyish yellow to pale orange (4B5–5A3). Colonies on CY20S white to yellowish white (1A1–2A2) or pale yellow in CCF 4914 and IBT 12659 (2A2–2A3), flat or centrally raised, radially wrinkled in some strains (CBS 266.81, CCF 4914 and IBT 12659), texture floccose, downy to velvety in CCF 4914 and IBT 12659, sporulation abundant, margins entire or diffuse, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse yellow to reddish yellow (3A6–4A6) or greyish yellow (4C5). Sporulation was abundant in all strains on all tested media except for strains NRRL 4847 (ex-type of A. albus var. thermophilus) and CCF 1649 which were sterile. Sclerotia were present on the colony surface after 4 wk of cultivation in strains CBS 266.81, CCF 3314, CCF 4914 and IBT 12659, absent in CCF 4030, CCF 4653, CCF 3853T, CCF 4658, CCF 6202, CCF 1649 and CCF 6397. Purple sclerotia were present only on CZA in all mentioned strains, no sclerotia were observed on MEA, CYA and CY20S. Purple sclerotia were present in both strains on CZA only.
Cardinal temperatures: Cardinal temperatures (on MEA, after 2 wk): Aspergillus neotritici does not grow at 10 °C, and its minimum growth temperature is 15 °C (4–13 mm). The optimum growth temperature is 30 °C (32–51 mm) and the maximum growth temperature is 40 °C (4–22 mm). No growth at 45 °C.
Ecology: Ecology (only records verified by DNA sequencing): The species is known from clinical samples, food (flour, corn, sunflower seed, cave cheese rind, grains of Triticum sativum), soil, indoor environments, outdoor air, vermicompost, and deep litter for pig raising. It has been reported in Brazil, China, Cuba, Czech Republic, India, Iran, Italy, South Africa, and the USA (Fig. 12, Table 1, Supplementary Table S3).

Macromorphology: Colonies growing fast CYA at 25 °C and 37 °C (diameter 70–85 mm after 7 days), producing purple-black, brown-black or black conidia. Colonies fast growing on all media. The colony reverse is cream- coloured dull yellow to yellow but may is some cases be dark brown to black. On CREA poor growth but with strong acid production. Sclerotia occasionally produced if raisins are added to an agar medium (Frisvad et al. 2014).
Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Chemical markers: Atromentins, fumonisins B2 and B4, funalenone, kotanin, malformins, naphtho- ?-pyrones, ochratoxin A (only 6–10 % of all strains examined), orlandin, pyranonigrin A-E, tensidol A &
Important mycotoxins: Fumonisins B2 and B4, ochra- toxin A (Frisvad et al. 2007, 2011, 2018).
Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus niger is common world-wide. It occurs on grapes, coffee, corn, onions, and many other foods. It also occurs in indoor air and in soils of potted plants.
Physiology: Aspergillus niger is halo-tolerant. It grows well at high temperatures; it can tolerate low pH values and rather low water activities. The black conidia are very radiation resistant and hence often found on sun-dried products.
Biotechnological applications: Production of citric acid, gluconic acid and oxalic acid. Used as a transformation host, especially for production of recombinant proteins. Production of amylases, lipases, pectinases, amyloglucosidases and many other enzymes. Used for production of awamori aquavit and Kuro- koji. Biotransformation of chemical compounds, waste handling, metal leaching and several other applications.
Biodeterioration and pathology: Produce a rot in grapes (black rot), onions and other fruits and vegetables. May degrade plastics, textiles and other materials. Opportunistic human pathogen (especially otomycosis).

Some strains produce conidial columns.
Similar species: Aspergillus oryzae resembles A. flavus. The former is more floccose, less strongly sporulating, has more smooth, larger and more brownish conidia. Aspergillus arachidicola differs by producing type B and G aflatoxins, while A. minisclerotigenes produces small
Synonym: Aspergillus gymnosardae A. oryzae var. effusus and several other varieties (see Frisvad et al. 2019)
Macromorphology: Colonies growing fast on CYA at 25 °C and 37 °C (diam. 70–85 mm after 7 days), producing pale greenish yellow conidia, later becoming light to dull brown. Colony texture floccose or rarely velutinous. Colonies fast growing on all media. The colony reverse is coloured creamish dull yellow to yellow. Sclerotia large, 400–700 µm, first white, then becoming black, often covered by exudate droplets, but only in few isolates. On CREA, poor growth and poor or no acid production. On AFPA a cream-coloured reverse.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Chemical markers: Asperfuran, asprirochlorin, cyclo- piazonic acid, kojic acid, 3-nitropropionic acid, penicillin, sporogen AO1. Odour usually weak.
Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus oryzae has only been found in industrial factories and is probably a domesticated form of A. flavus.
Physiology: Aspergillus oryzae is halo-tolerant. It grows well at high temperatures; it can tolerate rather low water activities.
Biotechnological applications: Aspergillus oryzae is used for fermentation of tuna fish (katsuobushi), production of soy sauce, production of sake, enzymes, especially amylases, as transformation host and several other purposes.

Diagnosis: Aspergillus pragensis is phylogenetically basal to A. subalbidus, A. tenebricus and A. taichungensis. Together with A. magnus, it is unique by its small colony diameters on all media, especially on CZA. Aspergillus pragensis and A. magnus can be easily distinguished by colony colour and strikingly different micromorphology (Fig. 5, Fig. 6). Aspergillus subalbidus, A. taichungensis, A. tenebricus and A. neotritici can be differentiated from A. pragensis by their ability to grow at 35 °C or higher temperatures (Table 6). Aspergillus pragensis differs from A. dobrogensis, A. magnus and A. campestris by its shorter and narrower stipes, shorter metulae and smaller vesicles (Table 5).

Culture characteristics: Culture characteristics (at 25 °C after 2 wk): Colonies on MEA white (3A1), slightly raised, crateriform in the centre, radially sulcate, texture velvety to downy, sporulation abundant, margins entire to slightly undulate, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse brownish yellow (5C6) in the centre, orange white (5A2) on the margins. Colonies on CYA white (3A1), centrally raised to umbonate, texture floccose to granular, sporulation abundant, margins entire or slightly undulate, exudate absent, soluble pigment dark brown in CCF 3962T, CCF 4654, CCF 5693, CCF 5847 after 4 wk (4–6 mm wide circle around colonies or in the area between colonies), reverse light brown to brownish orange (5D5–5C4). Colonies on CZA white (3A1) or brownish grey (4D2), flat, texture waxy to floccose, sporulation weak and located only in the colony centre, margins irregular or submerged, exudate absent, soluble pigment intense dark green to greyish blue in all strains after 4 wk (3–6 mm around colonies), reverse yellowish grey (3D2). Colonies on CY20S white (3A1) with a tint of yellowish white (3A2), flat to slightly raised, texture downy, granular or floccose, sporulation abundant, margins entire, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse light yellow (4A5). Sclerotia were present after 4 wk of cultivation in NRRL 58614 and CCF 5847, absent in CCF 3962T, CCF 4654 and CCF 5693. Dark brown to purple sclerotia covered by felt of mycelium were observed on CYA in NRRL 58614 and CCF 5847, and on MEA in CCF 5847. No sclerotia were observed on CZA and CY20S.
Cardinal temperatures: Cardinal temperatures (on MEA, after 2 wk): Aspergillus pragensis grows restrictedly at 10 °C (5–6 mm, colonies having character of minimally sporulating waxy drops) and the optimum growth temperature is 25 °C (15–18 mm). The maximum growth temperature is 30 °C (3–14 mm). No growth at 35 °C.
Ecology: Ecology (only records verified by DNA sequencing): The species is known from indoor environments (indoor air, carpet, dust), food (rice bran), clinical samples and outdoor air. It has been isolated in Canada, Czech Republic, South Korea and the USA (Fig. 12, Table 1, Supplementary Table S3).

Micromorphology: Ascomata single or borne in small clusters within loose white-creamish hyphae, globose, 200–300 µm in diam, with a multi-layered cell wall. Asci 8-spored, globose, 8–12 µm. Ascospores lenticular measuring 4.5–7.5 × 4.5–5 µm (including crests), with two widely separted equatorial crests of 1–2 µm and convex surface decorated with spinelike projections, ranging from less than 0.5 µm to as much as 2.0 µm. Phialides with a short neck, 6–8 × 2–2.5 µm covering the upper part of the vesicle. Conidia en masse blue-green coloured, globose to subglobose shaped, 2–3 ?m in diam, with a finely roughened wall.
Similar species: Aspergillus fischeri, A. hiratsukae and A. neoglaber are related foodborne species. For more details, see A. fischeri.
Synonym: Neosartorya fischeri var. spinosa N. spinosa
Macromorphology: Colonies growing fast on CYA at 25 °C and 37 °C (40–70 mm and 67–85 mm after 7 days, resp.), consisting of dense mycelium intermixed with ascomata and aerial hyphae bearing conidiophores. Conidial heads typically columnar; reverse colourless to light pink. Diameter on MEA 50–75 mm after 7 days at 25 °C, colonies white to pale yellow with granular appearance caused by a continuous layer of ascomata. On CREA poor growth and no acid production.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph known, neosartorya-type, homothallic.
Chemical markers: Aszonalenins, 2-pyrovoylamino- benzamide, pseurotin.
Habitats and distribution: Wordwide; pasteurized foods, soil, cardboard.
Physiology: Thermotolerant; good growth 37 °C. Aspergillus spinosus produces heat resistant ascospores that are able to survive a heat treatment.

Diagnosis: Aspergillus subalbidus is closely related to A. taichungensis and A. tenebricus. Aspergillus taichungensis differs from A. subalbidus by its larger colony diameters on MEA, CYA, CY20S, and by its pastel yellow colonies and yellow soluble pigment produced by some strains on CYA and MEA (Table 4). Aspergillus tenebricus has longer phialides and metulae than A. subalbidus. Aspergillus subalbidus differs from A. dobrogensis, A. magnus, A. neotritici, A. candidus and A. campestris by its shorter and narrower stipes and smaller vesicles (Table 5, Fig. 6). Aspergillus pragensis and A. magnus colonies have a smaller diameter compared to A. subalbidus. Aspergillus taichungensis and A. neotritici can be differentiated by their larger colony diameters at 37 °C and by their ability to grow at 40 °C (Table 6).

(4B4, 4B5, 4B6) or dark blond (5D4) in the centre, light yellow (4A4, 4A5) or golden brown (5D7) on margins, exudate absent, soluble pigment brown in some strains with varying intensity or location after 4 wk: central area between colonies in CCF 4913, CBS 112449, CCF 5697 and CBS 567.65T; 3–4 mm large circle around colonies in NRRL 58123 and CCF 5698; 5–6 mm large circle around colonies in CCF 5643; slightly pigmented areas around sclerotia in strain CCF 6199; rusty brown soluble pigment was present in strain CCF 6197 (6–7 mm around colonies). Colonies on CY20S white (4A1), yellowish white (2A2, 3A2, 4A2) or yellowish grey (4B2), flat or centrally raised, irregularly folded, texture floccose, less frequently granular, downy or fluffy, sporulation abundant, margins entire, less frequently erose or undulate, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse brownish orange (5C5, 5C6), light yellow (4A5), greyish yellow (4B4, 4B5, 4B6) or reddish yellow (4A6) in the centre, light yellow (4A4, 4A5) on margins. Sclerotia were produced superficially, less commonly covered by felt of mycelium (NRRL 4809 and CCF 6199 on CZA). After 4 wk of cultivation, they were observed in CBS 567.65T, NRRL 4809, FMR 15877, CCF 6197, CCF 6911, NRRL 5214 and CBS 112449, absent in CCF 5642, CCF 5696, DTO 196-E4, FMR 15733, CCF 4913, CCF 5848, CCF 5697, CCF 6205, CCF 5643, CCF 5698, NRRL 58123 and FMR 15736. Cardinal temperatures: Cardinal temperatures (on MEA, after 2 wk): Aspergillus subalbidus germinates or grows restrictedly at 10 °C (3–9 mm). The optimum growth temperature is between 25 °C (18–30 mm) and 30 °C (9–29 mm). Only eight out of 12 tested strains (CBS 567.65T, FMR 15736, NRRL 58123, FMR 15733, CCF 5643, NRRL 4809, CCF 5697, CCF 6197) were able to grow at 35 °C (2–22 mm) and only three out of 12 tested strains (CCF 5643, CCF 5697 and FMR 15733) were able to grow at 37 °C (3–9 mm). No growth at 40 °C.
Ecology: Ecology (only records verified by DNA sequencing): The species is known from indoor environments (indoor air, walls, dust, carpet, settle plates), caves, food (Chinese yeast cake, vegetable lard, agriculture products), dung, soil, and from the Dubia roach (Blaptica dubia). It has been isolated in Botswana, Brazil, China, Federated States of Micronesia, Germany, Ghana, South Africa, Spain, Thailand and the USA (Fig. 12, Table 1, Supplementary Table S3).

Micromorphology: Conidiophores hyaline or slightly coloured, smooth walled, 100–500 × 5–8 µm. Conidial heads radiate to nearly globose, 100–150 µm in diameter, biseriate. Conidiophore vesicles spathulate to subclavate, hyaline, 10–20 µm. Metulae 4–6(–7) × 2–3.5 µm, Phialides cylindrical with a short neck, 5–7(–10) × 2–3.5 µm. Similar species: Aspergillus sydowii is closely related to A. versicolor. The former species has blue green conidia and larger rougher walled conidia. Small reduced penicillate conidial heads are common in A. sydowii, but can also occur in A. versicolor. These structures may occur in other members of the Aspergillus versicolor clade.
Macromorphology: Colonies growing slowly on CYA at 25 °C (diameter 18–26 mm after 7 days), velvety, sometimes somewhat floccose, usually consisting of a dense felt of intensely blue green (“Delft blue”) conidiophores. Conidial heads blue green, radiate, exudate reddish brown often abundant. Reverse mostly in shades of reddish brown to dark red (maroon). On CREA good growth, but no acid production. Colonies on CYA at 37 °C: 2–16 mm in diameter after 7 days.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Chemical markers: Aspergillosenes, aspergillusones, aspermutarubrol, diorcinol, 4-hydroxy benzoic acid, expansols, fischeacid, fischexanthone, orcinol, sydo- nic acids, sydowinin A & B, sydowins, WIN64821, WIN 64745. Odour weak.
Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus sydowii is common world-wide, especially as a marine organism. However it has been found in foods, soil cotton, beans, nuts, straw, cotton fabrics, leather, paper, archives and in indoor air.
Physiology: Aspergillus sydowii is halo-tolerant and tolerates low pH.
Biodeterioration and pathology: Can cause sea fan disease and human mycoses.

Species description: Aspergillus taichungensis Yaguchi, Someya & Udagawa, Mycoscience 36: 421. 1995. MycoBank MB 434473.
Micromorphology: Conidial heads radiate, biseriate. Diminutive conidiophores present. Stipes (excluding diminutive) hyaline, smooth-walled, occasionally finely roughened, usually non-septate, occasionally with septa, (15–)40–90(–215) × (2–)3–4(–5) μm, vesicles hemispherical, elongated, subglobose or globose, (5–)7–11(–15) μm diam, metulae cylindrical or wedge-shaped (V-shaped), (4–)5.5–7(–9.5) μm long, covering three quarters to entire surface of vesicle; phialides ampulliform, (3.5–)4.5–5.5(–6.5) μm long. Conidia globose to subglobose, (2.5–)3–3.5(–4) (3.4 ± 0.3 μm) × (2.5–)3–3.5(–4) (3.2 ± 0.3 μm), smooth-walled, rarely finely verrucose.
Diagnosis: Aspergillus taichungensis has the shortest and narrowest stipes and smallest vesicles in section Candidi (Table 5, Fig. 6). It is micromorphologically most similar to A. tenebricus and A. subalbidus, but differs from these by its pastel yellow colonies, production of yellow soluble pigment by some strains on CYA and MEA, and by its shorter stipes, metulae and phialides, and smaller vesicles. In addition, colonies of A. taichungensis have a larger diameter on CYA and CY20S compared to A. tenebricus and A. subalbidus (Table 4). Aspergillus candidus, A. dobrogensis, A. magnus and A. pragensis can be differentiated by their inability to grow at 37 °C. Colonies of A. neotritici have a larger diameter than A. taichungensis at 37 °C and 40 °C (Table 6).
Holotype: PF1167. Culture ex-type: IBT 19404 = CCF 5597 = DTO 031-C6.
Culture characteristics: Culture characteristics (at 25 °C after 2 wk): Colonies on MEA pastel yellow (1A4), flat, texture floccose to granular or velvety, sporulation abundant, margins entire, exudate absent, soluble pigment yellow (all over the Petri dish, predominantly around colonies) present in DTO 266-G2 and IBT 19404T, reverse yellow (2A8, 3A6) or light yellow (2A5). Colonies on CYA pastel yellow (1A4) or pale yellow (1A3), flat, texture granular, sporulation abundant, margins entire to slightly undulate, exudate absent, soluble pigment yellow (all over the Petri dish) present in IBT 19404T and DTO 266-G2, reverse yellow (3B8) or deep yellow (4B8) with vivid yellow margins (3A8) or yellowish brown (5D5) with reddish yellow (4A6) margins. Colonies on CZA pastel yellow (1A4), flat, texture granular or waxy, sporulation weak and located in irregular zones, margins irregular, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse pastel yellow (1A4, 2A4). Colonies on CY20S white (2A1) with a tint of yellowish white (2A2), flat to centrally raised, texture granular, downy or floccose, irregularly folded, sporulation abundant, margins entire to slightly erose, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse light yellow (4A5) or reddish yellow (4A6). Sclerotia produced superficially, less commonly covered by felt of mycelium (DTO 270-C9 on CY20S). After 4 wk of cultivation, they were observed in strains DTO 270-C9 and IBT 19404T, absent in DTO 266-G2. Brown sclerotia were observed on CZA in strain IBT 19404T, and dark brown to black sclerotia on CY20S in strain DTO 270-C9. No sclerotia were observed on MEA and CYA.
Cardinal temperatures: Cardinal temperatures (on MEA, after 2 wk): Aspergillus taichungensis germinates or grows restrictedly at 10 °C (4–7 mm). The optimum growth temperature is between 20 °C (20–32 mm) and 25 °C (25–29 mm). Aspergillus taichungensis is able to grow at 37 °C (12–20 mm) and the maximum growth temperature is 40 °C (1–7 mm), but the strain IBT 19404T only germinates at this temperature (1–2 mm).
Ecology: Ecology (only records verified by DNA sequencing): The species is known from soil, agriculture products, caves and house dust. It has been isolated in Iran, Mexico and Taiwan (Fig. 12, Table 1, Supplementary Table S3).

Micromorphology: Conidiophores hyaline, long and coarse, 0.5–2 mm × 10–20 µm. Conidial heads radiate, splitting into separate columns, 500–600 µm in diameter. Conidiophore vesicles globose, 25–50 µm, metulae present, cylindrical 7–10 × 4–6 µm. Phialides cylindrical tapering to a distinct neck, 10–15 × 4–8 µm. Conidial heads often biseriate, but heads with only phialides also present. Conidia cylindrical to pyriform when young, later globose to subglobose, 5–6.5(–8) µm, conspicuously roughened from prominent tubercles and bars of brownish yellow colouring matter, the outer and inner conidial wall visible.
Similar species: Aspergillus tamarii resembles A. bertholletius (CBS 143687; CaM: JX198674), A. caelatus (CBS 763.97; CaM: MG518018), A. pseudocaelatus (CBS 117616; CaM: MG517995) and A. pseudotamarii (CBS 766.97; CaM: EF661521). The latter two species produce aflatoxins, while aflatoxins have never been found in A. caelatus and A. tamarii.
Macromorphology: Colonies growing fast on CYA at 25 °C and 37 °C (diameter 65–85 mm after 7 days), mostly sporulating densely, forming a dense felt of yellow-brown conidiophores, which rapidly turn dark green-brown. Colony texture is velutinous or more often with floccose tufts. Colonies fast growing on all media. The colony reverse is cream dull yellow to yellow to pinkish drab, but may in some cases be brown, especially in sclerotial strains. Sclerotia produced by some strains, brownish to purplish to black, large, 1–1.2 mm × 1.5–2 mm. On CREA poor growth and no or poor acid production. On AFPA a dark brown to maroon reverse.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Chemical markers: Aspirochlorin, (-)-canadensolide, cyclopiazonic acid, speradines, kojic acid. Odour usually weak.
Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus tamarii is pantropical. It occurs on amaranth, cacao, corn, spices, and other tropical raw material and products.
Physiology: Aspergillus tamarii is halo-tolerant. It grows well at high temperatures; it can tolerate rather low water activities.
Biotechnological applications: Tamari sauce.

Diagnosis: Aspergillus tenebricus is closely related to A. taichungensis and A. subalbidus. It has larger vesicles and longer phialides and metulae than A. taichungensis. Aspergillus tenebricus also produces a dark brown soluble pigment on CYA and CZA after 4 wk compared to A. taichungensis, which can produce a yellow soluble pigment on CYA and MEA. The length of phialides and metulae of A. tenebricus is comparable to A. dobrogensis, A. campestris and A. magnus but longer than other species (Table 5, Fig. 6). The colonies of A. taichungensis have a larger diameter than A. tenebricus on CYA and CY20S (Table 4). Aspergillus candidus, A. dobrogensis, A. magnus and A. pragensis can be differentiated by their inability to grow at 35–37 °C while colonies of A. neotritici and A. taichungensis have a larger diameter than A. tenebricus at 37 °C (Table 6).
Culture characteristics: Culture characteristics (at 25 °C after 2 wk): Colonies on MEA white (4A1) to yellowish white (4A2, 2A2), flat, texture floccose, sporulation abundant, margins slightly erose, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse greyish yellow (4B4). Colonies on CYA yellowish white (4A2), flat with slight radial folding, texture granular, sporulation abundant, margins entire, exudate absent, soluble pigment dark brown after 4 wk (3–6 mm large circle around colonies), reverse light yellow (4A5, 4A4) or dark blond (5D4). Colonies on CZA white (2A1) to yellowish white (2A2), flat, texture granular, sporulation abundant, margins entire, exudate absent, soluble pigment dark brown after 4 wk (3–5 mm large circle around colonies), reverse pale yellow (3A3). Colonies on CY20S white (2A1), flat, texture granular to floccose, irregularly folded, sporulation abundant, margins slightly erose or entire, exudate absent, soluble pigment absent, reverse greyish yellow (4C6) with pastel yellow (3A4) margins. Sclerotia were produced superficially and only on CZA after 4 wk of cultivation. Brown sclerotia were observed in strains DTO 440-E1 and DTO 337-H7T, and absent in DTO 440-E2. No sclerotia were observed on MEA, CYA and CY20S in any of the examined isolates.
Cardinal temperatures: Cardinal temperatures (on MEA, after 2 wk): Aspergillus tenebricus is able to grow at 10 °C (9–11 mm). The optimum growth temperature is 25 °C (26–33 mm). Strains DTO 337-H7T and DTO 440-E2 are able to grow at 37 °C (7–12 mm) in contrast to strain DTO 440-E1. No growth at 40 °C.
Ecology: Ecology (only records verified by DNA sequencing): The species is known only from soil. It has been isolated in Australia and South Africa (Fig. 12, Table 1).

Macromorphology: Colonies growing slowly on CYA at 25 °C (diameter 13–27 mm after 7 days), velvety, sometimes somewhat floccose, either consisting of a dense felt of conidiophores or of aerial hyphae and closely interwoven mycelium bearing the conidiophores. Colony colour at first white, then changing to yellow, orange-yellow to yellow green, often intermixed with flesh to pink colours. Reverse mostly in shades of cream yellow to reddish brown. Diameter on MEA 9–17(–22) mm after 7 days. On CREA good growth, but no acid production. Growth on CYA at 37 °C: 0(–6) mm diam. after 7 days.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Chemical markers: Aspergillus versicolor sensu lato produces anthcolins, aspercolins, aspergillitine, aspergillones, asperolactones, asperones, calbistrins A and C, cyclopiamin B, diorcinol, mycoversilin, rheoemodin, sterigmatocystin, versicolorins, versimide, versiol. Odour weak or earthy.
Habitats and distribution: Aspergillus versicolor is common world-wide. Common on cheese, cereals, soil, peanuts, nuts, spices, dry meat products. This species is common in indoor environments.
Physiology: Aspergillus versicolor is halo-tolerant and tolerates low pH. It can grow at lower temperatures than most other Aspergillus species.

Micromorphology: Ascomata are borne terminally on a pedicel, which is commonly up to 150 µm long (occasionally up to 1000 µm). The ascomata wall consists of hyphae and the ascomata are globose, 20–70 µm in diameter, subhyaline to brownish-red. Asci are globose to subglobose, 7.5–10 µm in diameter and the ascospores are yellowish ovate-ellipsoidal, often with a hyaline smooth wall, (4–)5–6 × 3–4 µm. The conidia are borne in basipetal succession in chains from undifferentiated conidiogenous cells. The conidia are ovate to pyriform with a broadly truncate base, 6–8(–11) × 5.5(–10) µm, mostly thin-walled, functioning as chlamydospores when thick-walled.
Similar species: Many similar species are described by differences in pigmentation and conidial size, but are insignificant for differentiation at species level (Li & Gou 2004, Stchigel et al. 2004). In the present concept, we regard these species to be synonyms of M. ruber. Monascus ruber is closely related to M. purpureus (Barbosa et al. 2017).
Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA or OAT at 25
Chemical markers: Citrinin, monacolins, monankarins, monascorubramine, rubropunctatin, monascin, moans- codilone, ankaflavin, monascopyridine.
Habitats and distribution: This species is cosmopolitan and typically found starch-rich food and feed, such as cooked potatoes, rice, seeds of oat, soya, sorghum, tobacco, olives, bread, silage, but also isolated from soil.
Physiology: This species can grow in a wide temperature range between 18 and 40 °C, and does tolerate low oxygen levels and low pH.
Biotechnological applications: Monascus has been used for fermentation and as food colouring agent for centuries in Asia. Monascus fermented rice products are sold as cholesterol-lowering agents due to the content of monacolins.

Species description: Paecilomyces fulvus Stolk & Samson
Micromorphology: Ascomata are white and up to 150 µm in diameter and ripening in 7 to 10 days at 30 °C. Wall lacking or very scanty, composed of loose wefts of hyaline, thin hyphae of about 1 µm in diameter. Asci are globose to subglobose, 9–12.5 µm in diameter and the ascospores are smooth walled, ellipsoidal and measure 5.0–7.0 × 3.0–4.5. Conidiophores up to 150 µm tall, smooth with phialides born in groups of two to five on short metulae and single phialides are occasionally born directly on the aerial hyphae. Phialides have a cylindrical basal portion, 12.5–17 × 2.5–3.5, and tapering abruptly to a long thin neck, 3–8.5 µm long and 1–1.2 µm in width. Conidia are produced in dry chains and usually cylindrical with flattened ends, 3.7–7.5 × 1.4–2.5 µm. Chlamydospores are usually absent, though occasionally detected in older cultures.
Similar species: Paecilomyces niveus and P. lagunculariae are similar species, but differ in size and shape of the conidia.
Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA or CYA at 30 °C reach a diameter of 50–90 mm in 7 days, composed of a basal felt with white ascomata, occasionally in localized sectors, covered by a velvety or floccose overgrowth of the conidial morph, which gives the colonies a yellowish brown appearance. Reverse colour is inconspicuous.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal, phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph produced in culture, homo- thallic.
Chemical markers: Byssochlamic acid (meriditin, ‘cy- cloaspeptide-like compound’).
Important mycotoxins: Paecilomyces fulvus is claimed to be a patulin producer, though Houbraken et al. (2006) showed that this mycotoxin is not produced by this spe- cies.
Habitats and distribution: This species is cosmopolitan and causes spoilage in pasteurized food products, such as fruit juices and canned strawberries. Paecilomyces fulvus is also commonly occurring in soil and this is often the primary source of spoilage incidents.
Physiology: The ascospores of this species are heat resistant (D90=4–36 minutes, Bayne and Michener 1979). Furthermore, P. fulvus grows well in atmospheres of 20– 60 % CO2 with 0.5 % O2 (Taniwaki et al. 2009) and is able to grow between 10 and 45 °C.

Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA or OA at 30 °C attaining a diameter of 60–90 mm in 7 days, consisting of a dense felt of numerous conidiophores giving the colonies a powdery yellow brown appearance. Reverse colour is inconspicuous.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal, phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph rarely produced in culture, heterothallic.
Chemical markers: Viriditoxin.
Habitats and distribution: Paecilomyces variotii is a common contaminant in air and often isolated from substrates originating from higher temperatures e.g. compost. Biodeterioration and pathology: Paecilomyces variotii is able to assimilate aromatic substrates and is isolated from toluene gas biofilters. This species is occasionally associated with human infections.

Penicillium bissettii and P. vasconiae share the production of red mycelia submerged in the media (Ramírez & Martinez 1980). Etymology: Latin, improvisum, meaning unexpected/unforeseen, named for the conidiophores, which have randomly arranged branches.
Notes: Phylogenetic analyses resolved P. improvisum, classiﬁed in section Aspergilloides, in a unique clade distinct from the 12 clades recognised by Houbraken et al. (2014) (Fig. 1, 2). Section Aspergilloides species are typically mono-verticillate, but some do produce extra subterminal branches as observed in some conidiophores of P. glabrum, P. armarii, P. athertonense and P. bussumense. In addition, more complex patterns occur in P. saturniforme (biverticillate), P. verhagenii (biverticillate and divaricate) and P. ranomafanaense (divari-cate). In common with the latter two, P. improvisum produces divaricate conidiophores. However, P. ranomafanaense and P. verhagenii produce rough-walled conidia in contrast to the smooth-walled conidia of P. improvisum. Additionally, P. ver-hagenii produces larger conidia (3.5–4 µm) than P. improvisum, while P. ranomafanaense has more ellipsoidal conidia in com-parison to the globose conidia of the new species.
Extrolites: citrinin, isofumigaclavine A, isofumigaclavine B.

CYA 25 °C, 7 d: Colonies moderately deep, raised at centre, radially sulcate; margins low, narrow, entire; mycelia white; texture velutinous; sporulation moderately dense, conidia en masse greyish turquoise (24D5–E5); soluble pigments absent; exudates absent; reverse greyish yellow (3B4), pale to yellowish grey (2A2–B2). MEA 25 °C, 7 d: Colonies low, plane; margins low, wide, irregular; mycelia white; texture velutinous; sporula- tion moderately dense, conidia en masse greyish turquoise to greyish green (24D4–E5–25E5); soluble pigments absent; exudates absent; reverse greyish yellow (2B3), greenish grey to dull green (1B2–29D4). The colony reverse is strong yellow, beige or pale cream. On MEA colonies rapidly growing with blue-green to green conidia, texture velvety and sometimes slightly floccose. On YES agar the degree of sporulation is strong, reverse colour yellow. The colonies are growing rapidly (diameter 40–65 mm, 7 days). On CREA poor to moderate growth with poor acid production.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph rarely produced in culture, heterothallic.
Chemical markers: Andrastin A & B, chrysogines (chrysogine, 2-pyruvoylaminobenzamide, 2-acetyl-quin- azolin-4(3H)-one & 2-(2-hydroxypropionylamino)-ben- zamide), citreoisocoumarins, 7-deacetoxyyanuthone, meleagrin, penicillins, PR-toxin, roquefortine C & D, sorbicillins (including bisorbibutenolide, bisorbicillinol, bisvertinoquinol, bisvertinolone, 2’,3’-dihydrosorbicil- lin, oxosorbicillinol tautomer, sorhinones A–C, rezisha- nones A–D, sorbicillin), xanthocillins.
Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. This species is, like P. chrysogenum, common in damp buildings and occurs frequently in indoor air, (house) dust and water-damaged building materials. Physiology: Penicillium rubens is halotolerant and psy- chrotolerant. It grows well from 5 to 30 °C and some isolates are able to grow slowly at 37 °C. The minimum water activity supporting growth of P. rubens is 0.82 and the optimum aw is between 0.96 and 0.98.
Biotechnological applications: Penicillium rubens is used for the production of penicillin.
Biodeterioration and pathology: Discoloration of building material.

The colony reverse is cream often with a brown center. On MEA the conidia are green and the granular to fasciculate colonies have a cream coloured reverse. Physiology: Penicillium verrucosum is psychro- and halo- tolerant. It grows well at low temperatures, but does not or poorly grow at 30 °C. It can tolerate low pH values and low water activities.

Macromorphology: Colonies on DRYES reach a diameter of 30–35 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing white and hairy. Reverse is reddish brown. Mycelium consisting of smooth to finely verruculose, hyaline to pale brown, branched, septate, 3–5 µm diam hyphae.

Macromorphology: Colonies flat, spreading, with mod- erate aerial mycelium. On PDA surface pale luteous with patches of olivaceous-grey, reverse pale luteous. On OA surface dirty white, reverse pale luteous. On MEA sur- face pale luteous, reverse luteous.

Habitats and distribution: Arthrinium spp. is wide- spread in commonly occurs as a saprobe on grasses, and also on leaves, stems and roots of a range of different plant substrates (Agut & Calvo 2004).

Species description: Aureobasidium melanogenum (Hermanides-Nijhof) Zalar et al.
Molecular markers: Aureobasidium melanogenum, ITS: FJ150886; ?-tubulin: FJ157858. Aureobasidium pullu- lans, ITS: FJ150906; ?-tubulin: FJ157869.
Micromorphology: Hyphae 2–16 µm in diam, hyaline, smooth- and thin-walled. In older cultures dark brown, thick-walled hyphae may be formed. These thick-walled hyphae may act as chlamydospores or often fall apart into separate cells (arthroconidia). Conidiogenous cells undifferentiated, intercalary or terminal on subhyaline hyphae or arising as short lateral branches. Blastic conidia produced synchronously in dense groups from indistinct scars or denticles (they can be produced all over the cell surface). Conidia one-celled, (7.5–)9–11(–16) × (3.5–)4–5.5(–7) µm, often with an indistinct hilum (= a mark or scar at the point of attachment), hyaline, smooth- walled. Secondary smaller conidia often produced. Endoconidia not common, but formed by an intercalary cell and released into a neighbouring empty cell.
Similar species: Aureobasidium pullulans is closely related with A. melanogenum. The colonies of the former species remain pink, light brown, or yellow for at least three weeks, while the colonies A. melanogenum become black or greenish-black quickly. The dark hyphae in A. melanogenum often fall apart into separate cells.
Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA at 24 °C attaining a diameter of 40 mm in 7 days, smooth, soon covered with a slimy mass of spores, yellow, cream, pink, brown or black. Aerial mycelium sometimes formed, scanty, thinly floccose.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal conidiogene- sis; sexual morph not known.
Typical cultures: Aureobasidium melanogenum: CBS 105.22; A. pullulans: CBS 100524
Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. Aureo- basidium species are saprophytes with a world-wide distribution. They have been isolated from soil, leaf surfaces of trees, such as oak, beech, maple and poplar and from rocks and monuments. They have been recorded from various foodstuffs, such as wheat-, barley- and oat grain, from flour, tomato, fresh harvested pecans, pears, grapes, fruit-juices and frozen fruit-cakes. Furthermore, they are also common in wet or water-damaged indoor environments, such as bathrooms, window frames, and have been isolated from human skin and nails.
Physiology: Aureobasidium melanogenum has a mini- mum at 10 °C, optimum at 30 °C, maximum at 35 °C. The maximum tolerated salt concentration is 10 %; Aureobasidium pullulans has other growth characteristics: minimum growth temperature of 4 °C, an optimum at 25
Biotechnological applications: Aureobasidium melano- genum is used a biofinish on wood; A. pullulans is known for its biotechnological significance as a producer of the biodegradable extracellular polysaccharide (EPS) pullu- lan (poly-?-1,6-maltotriose).
Biodeterioration and pathology: Weakly pathogenic to mammals.
References: Zalar et al. (2008), Slepecky & Starmer (2009), van Nieuwenhuijzen et al. (2016)

Species description: Botrytis cinerea Pers.
Molecular markers: DNA-dependent RNA polymerase subunit II: AJ745676; glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate de- hydrogenase: AJ705004; ITS: AJ745676.
Micromorphology: Conidiophores are frequently up to 2 mm and 16–30 µm wide, brown below, smooth-walled and with an apical head of alternate branches. Conidia are obovoid, 8–14 × 6–9 µm, usually with a protuberant hilum. They are pale brown, hydrophobic and smooth- walled. Microconidia produced on sporodochia (spermo- dochia), flask-shaped phialides often present, globose and 2.5–3 µm in diameter.
Macromorphology: Colonies at 20 °C attaining a diameter of 60 mm or more in 10 days on most media. Colonies are hyaline at first, later becoming grey to greyish brown. Sclerotia are black, consisting of a medulla and a dark brown to black cortical layer of cells and are extremely variable in shape and size.
Morphs: Asexual morph present holoblastic synchronous conidiogenesis; sexual morph produced on natural substrates, but not in culture.
Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. Botrytis cinerea has a world-wide distribution, but is mainly occurring in humid temperate and subtropical regions. It can be facultative parasitic on a wide range of plants. This so-called “grey-mould” can damage flowers, leaves, stems and causes fruit- and leaf-rot in grapes, strawberries, cabbage and lettuce. Also isolated from soils as well as stored and transported fruit and vegetables, contamination probably occurred already in the field.
Physiology: Conidium production can be stimulated growing the cultures on PCA and hay-infusion agar in near-UV (“black”) light. Optimum growth (21–)22–25(– 30) °C, minimum (-2–)5–12 °C and maximum (28–)33–
Biotechnological applications: “Noble rot” of grapes by B. cinerea. These grapes are subsequently used for the production of specific wine.
Biodeterioration and pathology: Botrytis cinerea is capable to spoil various types of fruits. The genus Botrytis comprises one generalist, B. cinerea, and this species is able to infect weakened or wounded plants. Other species are serious plant pathogens. Botrytis cinerea on grapes might also cause “winegrower’s lung”, a rare form of hypersensitivity pneumonitis (a respiratory allergic reaction in predisposed individuals).

Species description: Cadophora species
Molecular markers: Cadophora fastigiata, ITS: AY249073; elongation factor 1?: KM497087. Cadop- hora malorum, ITS: AY249059; elongation factor 1?: KM497090.
Micromorphology: Hyphae brownish, walls usually becoming distinctly encrusted with age. Phialides borne singly, laterally or terminally on the hyphae or in clusters, flask-shaped, brownish with a collarette, 6–10(– 30) × 2.2–3(–4.2) µm. Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor envi- ronments. This species is reported throughout Europe, North America, Uganda, Russia, New Zealand and Aus- tralia. Isolated from wood and wood pulp, soil, wheat, seeds of cultivated grasses.

Species description: Cephalotrichum gorgonifer (Bainier) Sandoval-Denis et al.
Micromorphology: Synnemata up to 3 mm tall, grey-brown, with a well-developed stipe and having an ellipsoidal or cylindrical sporulation portion. The ultimate synnematal branches bear the annellides and may give rise to curled sterile setae. Sterile setae subhyaline or brown, unbranched, coiled once or twice, even in diameter, variable in length and abundance, 150
Similar species: Five Cephalotrichum spp. are common in the built environment: C. domesticum, C. gorgonifer, C. microsporum, C. purpureofuscum and C. verrucisporum. A key to species is given on p. 44 of this book; C. domesti- cum phenotypically resembles C. purpureofuscum.

Species description: Cephalotrichum microsporum (Sacc.) P.M. Kirk
Micromorphology: Synnemata up to 1 mm tall, grey, with a slender sporulating portion, pointed when young, more rounded when sporulating to the tip. Annellides 4–9 × 3–4 µm in length. Conidia ovoid, truncated at one end, with a slightly pointed tip, smooth-walled, 3.5–5 × 2–3 µm.
Similar species: See C. gorgonifer.
Macromorphology: Colonies attaining a diameter of (10–)20–25(–30) mm on OA after 7 days at 25 °C; similar colony diameters on MEA and smaller colonies on DG18, 3–10 mm. Colony colour in sporulating areas green-brown or grey. Typical synnemata are lacking in young cultures (less than 7 days). Synnemata produced after prolonged incubation, and readily visible for the naked eye.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal, annellidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Habitats and distribution: Indoor. Cephalotrichum mi- crosporum has a worldwide distribution and is related to wet cellulose containing substrates, like wood. However, they can also occur on rotting plants, soil or dung.
Physiology: The optimum growth temperature is around 25 °C. No growth at 5 °C, reduced growth at 30 °C and no growth 37 °C.

Species description: Chaetomium cochlioides Palliser
Molecular markers: RNA-polymerase II second largest subunit (rpb2): KX976829; ?-tubulin (tub2): KX976949.
Micromorphology: Perithecia on PCA are superficial, brownish green to dull green sometimes with a yellow hue when viewed in reflective light. They are subglobose to ellipsoid, 200–440 µm in high and 140–420 µm in diameter excluding perithecial hair. Perithecial hairs are numerous, unbranched, septate, flexuous, loosely curled at the lower part and spirally coiled, which decrease in diameter towards the tip. They are dark brown and rough,
Similar species: Chaetomium coarctatum resembles C. cochliodes, especially the ascospore shape and the coiled hair, but the colonies of C. coarctatum are paler, the
Macromorphology: Colonies on OA and MEA reach diameters of 70+ mm at 25 °C in 7 days, appearing yellowish green with darker brownish green centre due to dense ascomata production. Ascomata (perithecia) are formed after 1 week in a dense layer on OA and MEA giving the colony an olive-greyish to brownish green appearance, but ascospores are first fully mature after 2 weeks. Colonies on PCA are 52–58 mm after 7 days with thin and yellowish mycelium and well separated olive grey perithecia. Colonies on DG18 reach a diameter of 19–25 mm in 7 days at 25 °C and have a greyish to yellowish white colour. No ascomata production on DG18.
Morphs: Asexual morph absent; sexual morph readily produced on OA, homothallic.

It has also been isolated from herbivorous dung.

Molecular markers: RNA-polymerase II second largest subunit (rpb2): KX976831; ?-tubulin (tub2): KX976952.

They are subglobose to obovoid, 280–440 µm in height and 255–380 µm in diameter excluding perithecial hair. Perithecial hairs are numerous, branched, septate, erect, flexuous and sometimes undulate. They are dark brown and verrucose, 3–5 µm at the base, repeatedly and dichotomously branched and tapering and fading towards the tip. Asci are clavate or fusiform, 36–49 × 12.5–16.5 µm with a 24–55 µm stalk and contain 8 ascospores. The asci disappear as the ascospores mature. The ascospores are brown when mature, broadly fusiform or lemoniform, usually apiculate in both ends. They are bilaterally flattened (10–)11.5–13.5(–16) × (8–)8.5–10(–11) × (6.5–)7–8

It is frequently detected on cellulose containing materials, such as gypsum wallboard, plywood, wallpaper, books, textile and cardboard, after severe water damage. It has also been isolated from herbivorous dung and straw.
Physiology: The optimum temperature for the production of ascomata is 18–24 °C and favoured by neutral pH and darkness. The ascospores are not heat resistant, but thermotolerant and can be very resistant to dry circumstances and UV irradiation. Growth and ascomata production, on the other hand, requires a high wateractivity.
Biodeterioration and pathology: Chaetomium elatum is able to deteriorate cellulosic materials, such as wet cardboard and plant material and can cause soft-rot in maple wood strips.

Species description: Cladosporium allicinum (Fr. : Fr.) Bensch et al.
Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA arise laterally from the agar surface. They can be up to 350 µm long, but are normally 20–330 µm and 3–5 µm wide with 5–8 µm wide swellings. Conidiophores are pale olive brown and smooth to slightly verrucose. They are straight sometimes with intercalary and terminal swellings and often with lateral or terminal branched. The ramoconidia are 34–40 × 3–4 µm with 0–2 septa. They are smooth and light brown in colour. The secondary ramoconidia are 10–24 × 3.5–5 µm and often aseptate. They are ellipsoid to subcylindrical and have 1 basal hilum and 1–2 distal hila carrying chains of often unbranched conidia. Intercalary conidia in the chains are ovoid to ellipsoid with a basal and a distal hilum, aseptate and 6–11 × 3–4 µm in size. The terminal conidia are ovoid to obovoid with a basal hilum, aseptate and 4–7 × 2.5–3.5 µm. All conidial types are pale brown in coloured and minutely verruculose to verrucose.
Similar species: Cladosporium allicinum belongs in the C. herbarum complex together with several similar species: C. herbaroides, C. herbarum and C. macrocarpum. Cladosporium herbaroides has similar conidial sizes, but more knotty conidiophores, C. herbarum has a looser terminal branching pattern, and C. macrocarpum has larger and more ornamented conidia.
Synonym: Cladosporium bruhnei Davidiella allicina Mycosphae- rella allicina
Macromorphology: Colonies on DRYES reach a diame- ter of 26–28 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing extremely folded and raised in the middle, velvety and dull spinach green to greyish green with a thin white rim. Reverse is dark. Colonies on MEA are 20 mm in diameter after 7 days. Colonies on DG18 have a diameter of 17–19 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing leaf green to greyish green also with a thin white rim, sulcate and downy.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, holoblastic acropetal conidiogenesis; sexual morph rarely produced in culture.
Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. Cladospo- rium allicinum is a common air-borne saprotroph, both indoors and outside, and is frequently encountered as a contaminant. It has been isolated from food sources such as cereal grain, living and decaying plant material, hypersaline and industrial waste water, from indoor environment sources such as water damaged wood and glass fibre and from human sputum and skin. Reported from most parts of the world.
Physiology: Cladosporium allicinum grows well in environments with fluctuating humidity.

Species description: Cladosporium cladosporioides (Fresenius) G.A. de Vries
Molecular markers: Elongation factor 1?: HM148244, HM148490; actin: HM148521.

Conidiophores are olive brown and verrucose at the basal end turning light brown and smooth at the top. They are straight without intercalary or terminal swellings and often branched. The first ramoconidia have a truncate base with no basal hilum. They are 20–30 × 3–3.5 µm with 1–3 distal hila and often aseptate. They are smooth and light brown in colour. The secondary ramoconidia are 12–45 × 3–3.5 µm and often aseptate. They are cylindrical and have 1 basal hilum and 1–2 distal hila carrying chains of often unbranched conidia. Similar species: Cladosporium cladosporioides is a complex and contains several species. Cladosporium pseudocladosporioides, which is very similar morphologically, has narrower ramo- and terminal conidia.
Macromorphology: Colonies on DRYES reach a diame- ter of 26–28 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing extremely folded and raised in the middle, velvety and dull spinach green to greyish green with a thin white rim. Reported from most parts of the world, but most often in temperate regions.

Species description: Cladosporium halotolerans Zalar et al.
Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA arise laterally from the agar surface. They can be up to 300 µm long, but are normally 20–50 µm long and 2.5–3 µm wide without swellings. Conidiophores are pale olive brown and smooth to slightly verruculose. They are straight sometimes with short lateral denticulate branching sites. Septa, which are sporadic, appear darker than the cell walls. True ramoconidia are rare. The secondary ramoconidia are (5–)7–12(–37) × (2–)2.5–3.5(–6.5) µm with 0(–1) septa. They are smooth to slightly verruculose and pale olive brown in colour. They are ellipsoid to subcylindrical and have 1 basal hilum and 1–4 distal conidiogenous loci carrying chains of often unbranched conidia. Intercalary and terminal conidia in the chains are globose to subglobose with a basal and a distal hilum, aseptate and (2–)3–4(–6) × (2–)2.5–3(–5) µm in size. They are dark brown, verrucose and aseptate.

Macromorphology: Colonies on DRYES reach a diameter of 26–28 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing extremely folded and raised in the middle, velvety and dull spinach green to greyish green with a thin white rim. Reverse is dark. Colonies on MEA are 20 mm in diameter after 7 days. Colonies on DG18 have a diameter of 17–19 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing leaf green to greyish green also with a thin white rim, sulcate and downy.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, holoblastic acropetal conidiogenesis; sexual morph no known.
Habitats and distribution: Indoor. Cladosporium halo- tolerans is the most common Cladosporium in the indoor environment and very often isolated from house dust. It is found both indoors and outside and is frequently encountered as a contaminant. It has been isolated from hypersaline water, from indoor environment sources such as water damaged bathroom and basement walls, gypsum wallboard, inner roofing in attics and from hu- man sputum and skin. It has also been found in gypsum sediment in Arctic ice and in rocks. Reported from all parts of the world.
Physiology: Cladosporium halotolerans is halophilic and can grow on MEA with 17 % NaCl. Its optimal growth temperature is 25 °C, but not at 4 or 37 °C. It can tolerate transient and fluctuating humidity and UV light.

Species description: Cladosporium herbarum (Pers.:Fr.) Link
Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA arise laterally from the agar surface. They are straight and sometimes branched. They are pale and smooth at the base turning greyish brown and minutely verrucose at the top. Conidiophores are up to 350 µm long, but mostly 70–150 × 3.5–4.5 µm and 3–5 µm wide, often geniculate with intercalary and terminal swellings 6–9 µm wide. The primary ramoconidia are straight or geniculate, 20–70 × 3.5–4 µm in size, several intercalary and distal conidiogenous loci. They are greyish brown and minutely verrucose with 3–6 septa. Their terminal swelling often holds 1–4 secondary ramoconidia that are aseptate, sometime having 1 septum, cylindrical with a truncate base and 15–25 × 5–7 µm in size. The intercalary conidia are 6–9 × 3–5 µm, cylindrical to fusiform and have up to 3 distal conidiogenous loci. Terminal conidia are aseptate, ellipsoid to obovoid, 4–6 × 3–4 µm in size. Ramo-, intercalary and terminal conidia are forming branched chains of 8–12 conidia giving a loose structure. All types of conidia are greyish brown and verrucose to verruculose.
Similar species: Cladosporium herbarum belongs in the C. herbarum complex together with several similar species: C. allicinum, C. herbaroides and C. macrocarpum. Cladosporium allicinum has straight conidiophores and a looser terminal branching pattern, C. herbaroides has similar knotty conidiophores, but smaller conidial sizes and C. macrocarpum has larger and more ornamented conidia.
Macromorphology: Colonies on DRYES reach a diameter of 27–30 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing folded, velvety and olive grey to lavender green with a white rim. Reverse is dark. Colonies on MEA are 9–18 mm in diameter after 7 days. Colonies on DG18 have a diameter of 22–23 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing dull greyish green (cactus green) with a white rim, slightly folded and downy.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, holoblastic acropetal conidiogenesis; sexual morph rarely produced in culture. Ascomata produce mature ascospores on axenic culture on water agar with nettle stems after a few months at 5–7 °C.
Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. Cladosporium herbarum has been isolated from food sources such as weathered cereal grain, mouldy fruit and vegetables, living and decaying plant material, cheeses, butter and margarine and from indoor environment sources such as water-damaged wood, wallpaper and plaster. It is possible that C. allicinum is more associated to indoor environments and C. herbarum to cereals and other food items. Reported from most parts of the world.
Physiology: Cladosporium herbarum is tolerant of environments and products with low water activity and can tolerate transient and fluctuating humidity and UV light.
References: Schubert et al. (2007), Bensch et al. (2012)

Species description: Cladosporium macrocarpum Preuss
Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA arise laterally from the agar surface. They are straight and sometimes branched. They are smooth to minutely verruculose and pale greyish brown turning paler at the top. The conidiophores are up to 250 µm long and 3–6 µm wide, geniculate, nodose with intercalary and terminal swellings 6–10 µm wide. True primary ramoconidia are rare. The lateral and terminal swellings of the conidiophore often holds 1–2 secondary ramoconidia each that are aseptate, sometimes having one septum, ellipsoidal to subcylindrical and 15–25 × 5–7 µm in size. They have 1 basal hilum and 2–4 distal conidiogenous loci. The intercalary conidia are 9–15 × 3–5 µm, cylindrical to fusiform and mostly aseptate. They sometimes have 1 septum and up to 3 distal conidiogenous loci. Terminal conidia are ellipsoid to obovoid, 4–10 × 3–5 µm in size, aseptate with 1 basal hilum. Ramo-, intercalary and terminal conidia are forming branched chains giving a loose structure and all types of conidia are greyish brown, verrucose to echinulate and have darker and thickened walls and septa.

Macromorphology: Colonies on DRYES reach a diameter of 27–29 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing sulcate, velvety and greyish white. Reverse is dark. Colonies on MEA are 20 mm in diameter after 7 days. Species description: Cladosporium sphaerospermum Penzig
Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA arise laterally from the agar surface. They can be up to 300 µm long, but are normally 45–130 µm and 3–4 µm wide. Conidiophores are light brown and smooth at the basal end turning olive brown and finely verrucose at the top. They are straight without intercalary or terminal swellings. The first ramoconidia have a truncate base with no basal hilum. They are 20–45 × 3–3.5 µm with 2–6 septa and 1–3 distal hila. The secondary ramoconidia are 16–25 × 3 µm with 1–5 dark and pronounced septa. They are cylindrical and have 1 basal hilum and 1–2 distal hila carrying chains of often unbranched conidia. Intercalary conidia in the chains are dark brown fusiform with 1 basal and 1–2 distal hila, aseptate and 5–5.5 × 3–3.5 µm in size. The terminal conidia are globose to subglobose, aseptate and 3–4 × 3–3.5 µm. Intercalary and terminal conidia are dark olive brown in coloured and verrucose.
Similar species: Cladosporium sphaerospermum belongs in the C. sphaerospermum complex together with several similar species. C. sphaerospermum and C. halotolerans have very similar micromorphology, but C. sphaerosper- mum has ramoconidia with thick dark septa.
Macromorphology: Colonies on DRYES reach a diameter of 23 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing sulcate, velvety and olive green to olive yellow. Reverse is dark. Colonies on MEA are 8–18 mm in diameter after 7 days. Colonies on DG18 have a diameter of 19–23 mm in 7 days at 25 °C, appearing greyish green to dull green, slightly folded and downy.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, holoblastic acropetal conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. Cladospo- rium sphaerospermum has occasionally been isolated from fruit and grain, but it is very commonly isolated from in- door environment sources such as water-damaged wood, plaster, paint, textiles and gypsum wallboard. Reported from most parts of the world.
Physiology: Cladosporium sphaerospermum is tolerant of environments with low water activity and can tolerate transient and fluctuating humidity and UV light.
References: Zalar et al. (2007); Bensch et al. (2012; 2018)

Species description: Coniochaeta hoffmannii (J.F.H. Beyma) Z.U. Khan et al.

Phialides either single on hyphae or in dense clusters on short lateral branches, or intercalary along undifferentiated hyphae, hyaline, cylindrical to flask–shaped, sometimes elongate, 7–20 µm long, or subglobose to ovoid, 3–7 × 2–3 µm; intercalary phialides cylindrical with one or several scattered collarettes.
