Species description: Curvularia geniculata (Tracy & Earle) Boedijn
Micromorphology: Conidiophores erect, pigmented becoming paler near the tip, sometimes geniculate up to 600 µm long, septate. (Poro)conidia usually 4-septate, mostly curved unilaterally at the broadest and most pigmented central cell, adjacent cells less pigmented and the end cells subhyaline, 18–35(–37) × 8–14 µm. Heterothallic.
Macromorphology: Colonies, PCA and OA moderately fast growing, reaching a diameter of 30–40 mm within a week at 25 °C, brownish black, velvety sometimes becoming somewhat cottony. Reverse brown.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, enteroblastic conidio- genesis (poroconidia); sexual morph known but rarely produced in culture.
Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. Curvularia species have a world-wide distribution. They have been isolated from soil and plant materials with a preference for the tropics and warmer climates. Curvularia geniculata is also frequently isolated from cellulosic materials, e.g. paper, archives.
Physiology: Sporulation is enhanced by incubation under near-UV light.

Species description: Didymella macrostoma (Mont.) Q. Chen & L. Cai
Micromorphology: Pycnidia superficial on or immersed in agar, globose-oval, 80–260 µm diam, blackish brown, with one (occasionally two) distinct ostiole of 10–30 µm in diam. Species description: Epicoccum nigrum Link
Micromorphology: Pulvinate sporodochia appearing in 8–10 days on SNA, visible as black spots, 100–2000 µm in diam. Conidiophores in clusters, straight or more or less flexuous, terminating in more or less isodiametric conidiogenous cells, colourless to pale brown, short, 5–15 × 3–6 µm. (Blasto)conidia formed singly, globose to pyriform, commonly 15–25 µm in diam, with funnel- shaped base and broad attachment scar, often with pale protuberant basal stalk cell, dark golden brown, verrucose, obscuring the septa which divide the conidia into up to 15 cells.
Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA or OA at 20 °C attaining a diameter of at least 60 mm in 10 days, lanose to felty, yellow-orange, red or brown, sometimes greenish. Reverse similar, often more intensely coloured.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, holoblastic conidioge- nesis; sexual morph not known.
Physiology: Temperature: optimum 23–28 °C; minimum (-3–)4 °C; maximum 45 °C. Cultures often remaining sterile, sporulation, can be induced by exposure to near- UV (“black”) light.

Species description: Exophiala species
Micromorphology: The so-called “black yeasts” have melanin deposits in their cell wall, and many of them are capable of forming a synanamorph consisting of abundant septate mycelium. Exophiala is the main genus of blackyeasts, characterisedbyannellidic conidiogenesis. Conidiogenous cells intercalary, cylindrical, or free, flask shaped or acicular, with relatively narrow, short or very short annellated zones. Conidia formed percurrently in slimy heads, (sub)hyaline, smooth-walled, 1–4 celled. Often chains of spherical cells are formed which bud profusely. Chains of barrel-shaped hyphal cells may be present. Chlamydospores or sclerotial bodies occassionally formed.
Macromorphology: Colonies mosty restricted, slimy at the centre due to yeast-like growth, smooth near the margin, later often becoming velvety or lanose, olivaceous black.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, combination of acropetal and basipetal annellidic conidogenesis; sexual morph rarely produced.
Habitats and distribution: Exophiala is commonly occurring and has previously been isolated from water (both tap and bottled), wet indoor environments, soil, plants and decaying wood material. Multiple species are related to tap and bottled water, and these include E. angulospora, E. aff. pisciphila, E. oligosperma and E. xenobiota. Members of the resembling genus Cladophialophora are encountered in sugared drinks (e.g. C. potulentorum, C. australiensis and C. subtilis).
Physiology: Intolerant to 10 % NaCl and benomyl; lac- tate, inulin and citrate mosly not assimilated.
Biodeterioration and pathology: Exophiala is the causative agent of various human infections.
References: de Hoog et al. (2000), Baldadi et al. (2008)

Species description: Fusarium avenaceum (Corda) Sacc.
Molecular markers: ?-tubulin: AF405461. ITS: U26738. Elongation factor 1?: AY337423. Strains of this species have been full genome sequenced (Lysøe et al. 2014).
Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA are simple or branched, arising from the aerial mycelium often in orange sporodochia with simple or proliferated monophialides. Microconidia from polyblastic conidiogenous cells are fusiform, 0–3-septate, variable in size, 6–30 × 2.5–4.5(–6) µm. Macroconidia borne on phialides are narrowly fusiform, slender or sickle-shaped to almost straight having 4–7 septa with an elongated apical cell and a distinct foot cell, mostly 35–90 × 3.5–4(– 6) µm. Conidia in mass are more or less orange coloured. Chlamydospores are absent in mycelium, but sometimes present in conidia.
Similar species: This species belongs to the “Fusarium tricinctum species complex”. Fusarium arthrosporioides has a similar colony appearance on PDA and YES but does also produce pyriform microconidia. The PDA and YES colonies of F. tricinctum may resemble F. avenaceum, but F. tricinctum has much shorter macroconidia and lacks  the  septated  fusiform  microconidia.  Fusarium
Macromorphology: Colonies on PDA at 25 °C reach a diameter of 30–60 mm in 4 days. This species can be extremely variable in appearance and colour, commonly yellowish or reddish with a whitish floccose overgrowth of aerial mycelium. The latter becomes peach-coloured or reddish-brown and velvety with age. Reverse is yellowish or brownish often with reddish shades. Colonies on YES at 25 °C have a diameter of 30–60 mm after 4 days with a velvety light-brownish or reddish mycelium, often with dark brownish to black sclerotium-like structures. The reverse is light to dark brown sometimes with a reddish shade.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph rarely produced.
Chemical markers: 2-amino-14,16-dimethyloctade- can-3-ol, antibiotic Y, aurofusarin, chlamydosporol, chrysogine, enniatins, fusarin C, gibepyrone A, monili- formin.
Habitats and distribution: Frequently occurring on cereal grains, vegetables and many other food items as well as in agricultural soils. World-wide distribution, mainly in temperate zones, but also reported from warmer or subtropical regions.
Biotechnological applications: Has been evaluated as a potential bio-control agent of knapweed, and to control wild raspberry and related invasive Rubus species.
Biodeterioration and pathology: Causes root rots in cereal plants (e.g. wheat, rye, barley, maize), clover, lucernes. Damage vegetables and fruits such as peaches, apples, pears as well as stored seeds of oats, barley, and wheat.

Species description: Fusarium culmorum (W.G. Smith) Sacc.
Molecular markers: ?-tubulin: AF212779. ITS: AY260958. Elongation factor 1?: AF212463 .
Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA are usually branched with short and wide phialides from which rather thick-walled macroconidia are borne in the aerial mycelium often in sporodochia or in pionnotes with a red- brown slime. Microconidia are absent. Macroconidia are fusiform to sickle-shaped, usually 5-septate (sometimes 3–4- or 6–8-septate), with a more or less pointed apex and a distinct footcell, 3-septate: 26–36 × 4–6 µm, 4-septate: 30–46 × 5–7 µm, 5-septate: 34–50 × 5–7 µm. Chlamydospores are brownish, smooth to rough-walled and present in mycelium or in conidia. Sometimes they are present in chains or in clumps. Some cultures do not form chlamydospores.
Similar species: This species belongs to the “Fusarium sambucinum species complex”. Colonies on PDA and YES
Macromorphology: Colonies on PDA at 25 °C reach a diameter of 75–90 mm in 4 days with a floccose aerial mycelium. At first the mycelium is white to yellowish turning into pinkish, red ochraceous to brownish- red. Reverse and agar surface is reddish to purple or brownish. Colonies on YES at 25 °C have a diameter of 75–90 mm after 4 days with a sparse aerial mycelium. Colonies are velvety in ochre to brownish-red shades. Reverse is yellowish brown to dark brown, sometimes with a reddish tinge.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Chemical markers: 2-acetylquinazolinone, aurofu- sarin, butenolide, chrysogine, culmorin, fusarin C, rubrofusarin, trichothecenes (deoxynivalenol, 3- and 15-acetyldeoxynivalenol, fusarenon X, nivalenol and de- rivatives hereof.), zearalenone.
Important mycotoxins: Deoxynivalenol and other tri- chothecenes, fusarin C, zearalenone.
Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor environments. World-wide distribution with a preference for the temperate zones. Occurring on grains and stems of oats, barley, wheat, and other cereals, agricultural soils.
Biodeterioration and pathology: Causes foot and root rot and head blight in cereals. Attacks maize plants and cobs and causes storage rot of apples, potatoes, sugar beet.

Species description: Fusarium equiseti (Corda) Sacc.
Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA are often branched and monophialidic. Microconidia absent or rare, spindle-shaped or ovoid, 0–2-septate, 6–24 × 2.5–4 µm. Macroconidia sparse at first and borne from simple lateral phialides on the aerial mycelium. Macroconidia are sickle-shaped with a distinct foot cell and in some isolates an elongated curved apical cell, 3–5(–7)-septate, typically 5-septate. 3-septate: (15–)22–45 × (2.5–)3–5 µm, 5-septate: (30–)40–60 × (3–)3.7–5 µm, 7-septate: 42–60 × 4–6 µm. Chlamydospores are abundantly pro- duced intercalary, solitary, in chains or clumps, in the hyphae or in conidia. They are pale brown at maturity and often with a rough cell wall.
Similar species: This species belongs to the “Fusarium incarnatum-equiseti species complex”, which is poorly resolved with many undescribed phylogenetic species (O’Donnell et al. 2013, Villani et al. 2016). The conidium morphology is quite variable. Isolates from temperate area tend to have conidia with a short bended tip, whereas
Macromorphology: Colonies on PDA at 25 °C reach a diameter of 45–70 mm in 4 days with floccose aerial cream to yellowish-brown mycelium. A tendency towards pionnotes and sporodochia can be observed in some isolates. Reverse is peach-coloured, changing to light- brown or dark-brown. Species description: Fusarium graminearum Schwabe
Molecular markers: ?-tubulin: AF212776. Elongation factor 1?: AF212459 . Several strains of this species have been full genome sequenced.
Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA are at first simple monophialides on the hyphae later strongly branched. Microconidia are absent. Macroconidia are slender, sickle-shaped, curved with pointed and curved apical and pedicellate cells, mostly (3–)5–6(–9)-septate, 41–60 (–80) × 4–5.5 µm. Chlamydospores are sometimes present, mostly intercalary and in chains, but often absent. Sporulation is often sparse (induction by near UV-light). Similar species: This species belongs to the “Fusarium graminearum species complex” that contains morphological indistinguishable species. Macromorphology: Colonies on PDA at 25 °C are growing fast with a diameter of 75–90 mm after 4 days. The colony is greyish rose, red to bluish-red, becoming brownish at age. The aerial mycelium is floccose and whitish becoming brownish to rose. Reverse in red to reddish brown shades. Colonies on YES at 25 °C have a diameter of 75–90 mm after 4 days with a sparse aerial mycelium. Colonies are velvety in ochre to brownish- red shades. Reverse is yellowish brown to dark brown, sometimes with a reddish tinge.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph has been observed and may occur in cultures.
Chemical markers: 2-acetylquinazolinone, aurofusa- rin, butenolide, chrysogine, culmorin, fusarin C, rubrofusarin, trichothecenes (deoxynivalenol, 3- and 15-acetyldeoxynivalenol, fusarenon X, nivalenol and derivatives hereof), zearalenone.
Habitats and distribution: Food. World-wide distri- bution, and is a colonizer and sometimes a parasite of mainly graminaceous plants. Reported from soil, cereal grains and seeds of grasses.
Biotechnological applications: A strain designated A 3/5 used for production of Quorn® mycoprotein was originally identified as F. graminearum, but has been reidentified as F. venenatum. This strain has been used as a host for heterologous protein production using the misapplied name F. graminearum.
Biodeterioration and pathology: F. graminearum causes foot and root rot and head blight in cereals. It often attacks maize plants and cobs.

Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA are often branched bearing monophialides. Chlamydospores occur in hyphae or in conidia, hyaline, smooth- or rough-walled, (sub)globose, 5–15 µm in diameter, terminal or intercalary, in chains, pairs or single.
Similar species: This species belongs to the “Fusarium oxysporum species complex” that is poorly resolved with many undescribed phylogentic species. F. oxysporum is very variable in culture and morphology and may also be confused with F. subglutinans and Neocosmospora solani. Several species has been proposed based on phylogenetic
Macromorphology: Colonies on PDA at 25 °C reach a diameter of 30–55 mm in 4 days. The aerial mycelium is sparse or floccose to velvety, whitish or peach, usually with a purple tinge. In some strains orange sporodochia may occur. The reverse is yellowish or in purple shades. Colonies on YES at 25 °C have a diameter of 30–60 mm after 4 days with a velvety appearance. The mycelium is whitish to light yellowish, some colonies dark rose to purple. The reverse is yellowish or in purple shades.

Physiology: The species can grow under anaerobic conditions. Some strains may grow at 37 °C or slightly higher.
Biotechnological applications: Fusarium oxysporum is a useful producer of enzymes used for bio-ethanol pro- duction, and is also used as a bio-control agent in agri- culture.
Biodeterioration and pathology: Occurring mainly as a soil saprophyte but can be pathogenic to numerous plants causing wilt. Causes storage rot (e.g. in maize, beet). Pathogenic to humans (keratitis).
References: Di Pietro et al. (2003), Leslie & Summerell (2006), O’Donnell et al. (2013)

Molecular markers: ?-tubulin: U34468. ITS: X94166. Elongation factor 1?: AY337450. This species have been full genome sequenced.
Micromorphology: Conidiophores on SNA are mostly unbranched, formed on aerial mycelium, with 1–3 simple elongated phialides. Microconidia are produced in long chains (can be observed in Petri-dish under low power), rarely in false heads, mostly one-celled, clavate with a truncate base, 4.3–20 × 1.5–4.5 µm. Chlamydospores are absent. When present sclerotia are blackish-blue and probably perithecial initials.

Macromorphology: Colonies on PDA at 25 °C have a diameter of 35–55 mm in 4 days peach and are pale cream, violet to lilac. The aerial mycelium is dense, delicately floccose to velvety or with a powdery appearance due to microconidia production and often in white, rose to vinaceous colours. Sporodochia are rarely formed. The reverse in dark violet, lilac, vinaceous or in light shades. Colonies on YES at 25 °C have a diameter of 30–60 mm after 4 days with a velvety appearance, typically in dark rose to purple shades. Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph has been been observed and usually occur only on dead plant material.

Species description: Geotrichum candidum Link
Micromorphology: Advancing hyphae septate, dicho- tomously branched (forked), 7–11 µm wide. Conidia cylindrical, barrel-shaped or ellipsoidal, mostly 6–12(– 20) × 3–6(–9) µm, formed by breaking up fertile hyphae, chains mostly aerial, erect or decumbent.
Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA attaining a dia- meter of 70 mm in 7 days at 24 °C, white, smooth, often butyrous or membranous, odour often sweet. Colonies very restricted on DG18.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, thallic conidiogenesis, sexual form sometimes present.
Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. This species has a worldwide distribution, and has been isolated from various substrates, such as soil, water, air, corn and other cereals, rice, grain, rotting paper, textiles, grapes, citrus, bananas, tomatoes, cucumber, frozen fruitcake, fruit juices, bread, milk and milk products, animals and man. This species is also known as the “white milk fungus” or “machinery mould”.
Physiology: Geotrichum candidum has, like many types of yeast, a preference for moist or wet environments. Growth occurs at a water activity of 0.95, and no growth is observed at 0.90. The optimum growth temperature is 25–27 ° and the maximum is between 35–38 °C.
Biotechnological applications: Recent surveys indicate that G. candidum can play an important role in the ripening of many soft and semi-hard cheeses and make a positive contribution to the development of taste and aroma. It may also influence the growth of other microorganisms, both valuable and detrimental.

Species description: Gliomastix murorum (Corda) S. Hughes
Micromorphology: Hyphae bearing phialides are often aggregated into ropes. Conidiophores are poorly defined, consisting of 1–3 cells. Phialides hyaline and smooth below, becoming subhyaline to olivaceous brown and sometimes roughened with discrete granules towards the apex, 10–35 × 1.5–3.5 µm, below tapering slightly to 0.7–1.5 µm at the apex, which very occasionally has a tiny flared collarette. Conidia produced in slime and forming readily seceding chains, often with conspicuous separators between the spores, non-septate, subglobose to ellipsoidal, thick-walled, usually markedly roughened, dark olivaceous brown to black, 2.3–5.5 × 2.0–4.5 µm wide, mostly 3.0–3.5 µm.
Similar species: The difference between G. murorum var. murorum having catenate conidia and G. murorum var. felina having conidia in slimy heads does not appear to be supported by phylogenetic analysis. Therefore these varieties are considered under G. murorum (Summerbell et al. 2011) Gliomastix polychroma also occurs in indoor environments and produces conidia in dry chains.
Macromorphology: Colonies on OA attaining a diameter of 12–22 mm after 7 days at 25 °C; on MEA slightly smaller, 8–18 mm, on DG18 3–9 mm. Colonies of young cultures (less than 7 days) on MEA are white with some floccose mycelium and becoming olivaceous- black with age due to sporulation; usually with extensive feathery mycelial ropes, especially in fresh isolates. Reverse on MEA pink-brown or brown.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Habitats and distribution: Worldwide, isolated from soil and various plant materials, but also from cellar wall, swimming pool floor, cereals, fruit (apple, banana).
References: Domsch et al. (2007) under Acremonium murorum, Summerbell et al. (2011)

Species description: Lichtheimia corymbifera (Cohn) Vuill.
Micromorphology: Stolons 5–20 µm in diameter, often with adhering droplets, hyaline to brownish, smooth- walled, with an occasional septum, often terminating in a large sporangium. Rhizoids borne on a swollen area of the stolon, up to 370 µm long, infrequently branched. Sporangiophores (40–)80–450(–500) × (3–)4–8(–13) µm, hyaline to faintly pigmented, smooth to slightly roughened, simple or sometimes branched, arising solitarily from the stolons, in groups of three or up to 7 in a whorl below the large terminal sporangium at some distance from the rhizoids (smaller sporangiophores also bent or circinnate). Sporangia more or less pyriform, 10–40 µm in diam, up to 80 µm when terminating a stolon, many-spored, hyaline at first, becoming grey to greyish-brown when mature; wall transparent, smooth to slightly roughened. Columella hyaline to greyish, with or without a collar, (7–)10–30 µm in diam, up to 60 µm when terminating a stolon, globose to short ovoid (especially larger ones). The apex of smaller columellae often with one to several projections. Sporangiospores varying from subglobose to oblong-ellipsoidal, (2.5–)3– 6(–7) × 2.5–4.5 µm, hyaline to light grey, smooth-walled.
Macromorphology: Colonies growing rapidly, covering the whole Petridish within one week. Fast growth at both 25 and 37 °C. Colonies light greyish, 5–7 mm high (up to 15 mm).
Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. World- wide distribution with a preference for (sub)tropical regions. This species has been isolated from soil, stored grain, decaying vegetables, fruit, air, compost, animals and man.
Physiology: Optimum temperature between 35–37 °C; maximum 45 °C.
Biodeterioration and pathology: Lichtheimia corym- bifera is an uncommon agent of human (sub)cutaneous mycosis and several cases of invasive infections in AIDS patients have been published. It is the most frequent agent of bovine mycotic abortion (de Hoog et al. 2000).

Species description: Mucor circinelloides van Tieghem

Sporangiophores filled with droplets in younger parts. Sporangia whitish to yellowish at first becoming brownish-grey when mature, up to 80 µm in diam (rarely 100 µm), walls slightly roughened (spinulose), walls of larger sporangia leaving small collars after breaking up, walls of smaller ones persistent and leaving large basal membranes. Similar species: Mucor circinelloides differs from M. racemosus by the absence of chlamydospores.

Biotechnological applications: Mucor circinelloides has been detected, together with Mucor indicus and Amylomyces rouxii, in various fungal fermented food products from the Orient.

Species description: Mucor plumbeus Bonorden
Micromorphology: Sporangiophores with slightly encrusted walls, branching (sympodial and monopodial) up to 20(21) µm in diam, constricted and somewhat recurved below the sporangium. Sporangia hyaline becoming dark-brown to brownish-grey with age, up to 80(–100) µm in diam with spinulose walls. Columellae pyriform, obovoid with a truncate base or ellipsoidal to cylindrical-ellipsoidal; smaller columellae often pointed- conical, up to 25–50 µm (seldom up to 50–70 µm), hyaline becoming brown to grey, smooth or roughened often with several projections, collar present. Sporangiospores globose, sometimes more or less ellipsoidal or irregularly shaped, (5–)7–8(–10) µm in diam, yellowish-brown, slightly rough-walled. Chlamydospores present, especially in older cultures. Heterothallic. Zygospores rare.
Similar species: Mucor plumbeus is easily recognisable by its columellae with projections.
Macromorphology: Colonies fast growing, covering the Petri dish within one week, grey or light olive-grey coloured, variable in height (between 2–20 mm), due to strain properties and to external conditions (media, temperature).
Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor, often as air contaminant. World-wide distribution, e.g. soils, hay, dung, stored seeds of wheat, oats. This species is dimor- phic and can grow,under anaerobic conditions in a yeast phase (e.g. in juices).
Physiology: Growth and sporulation at 5–20 °C (at 5 °C slow); growth but poor sporulation between 20–30 °C and no growth at 37 °C.

Species description: Mucor racemosus Fresenius
Micromorphology: Sporangiophores branched (in a mixed sympodial and monopodial way), the short branches sometimes recurved, with encrusted walls. Sporangia hyaline becoming brownish to grey with age, up to 80(90) µm in diam but mostly 70 µm in diam, wall spinulose (small sporangia up to 20 µm in diam with persistent walls). Columella obovoid, ellipsoidal, cylindrical-ellipsoidal, slightly pyriform, usually with truncate base, up to 37–55 µm, light brown with collar. Sporangiospores broadly ellipsoidal to subglobose, 5.5– 8.5(–10) × 4–7 µm or 5.5–7 µm in diam, smooth walled, greyish. Chlamydospores numerous, in sporangiophores and sometimes in columellae, barrel-shaped when young, subglobose in older cultures, yellowish. Heterothallic. Zygospores (after 10 days on cherry agar at 10 °C) in aerial mycelium, reddish-brown to bright-brown, globose or subglobose, up to 110 µm in diam, roughened by short spines (5 µm in length); suspensors equal or subequal, up to 33 µm long and 35 µm wide; zygospores slightly roughened. Chlamydospores can be present in zygophores and suspensors.
Similar species: Mucor racemosus is similar to M. circinelloides, but the former is characterised by the formation of numerous chlamydospores in sporangiophores (and sometimes columellae).
Macromorphology: Colonies fast growing, covering the Petri dish within one week, white, becoming brownish- grey with age, 2–20(–30) mm in height, consisting of tall and short sporangiophores.
Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. World-
Physiology: Good growth and sporulation between 5–30 °C; optimum 20–25 °C and maximum around 37 °C.
Biodeterioration and pathology: Mucor racemosus is responsible for a spongy soft rot of cool stored (sweet) potatoes and citrus.

Species description: Neocosmospora solani (Mart.) L. Lombard & Crous
Molecular markers: Elongation factor 1-alpha: KT313611; DNA-dependent RNA polymerase subunit II: KT313623.
Micromorphology: onidiophoreson SNA areunbranched or branched bearing monophialides. Microconidia are usually abundant, ovoid or oblong, 0–1-septate, 8–16(– 24) × 2–4(–5) µm, formed from elongated (up to 90 µm) and sometimes verticillate conidiophores. Macroconidia formed after 4–7 days from short branched conidiophores which may form sporodochia, 3–5(–7)-septate (usually 3-septate), fusiform, cylindrical, often moderately curved, 27–52(–65) × 4.4–6.8 µm, with an indistinctly pedicellate footcell and a short blunt apical cell. Chlamydospores are hyaline, smooth- or rough walled, globose to ovoid, in hyphae or in conidial cells, either terminal, on lateral branches, intercalary or in chains.
Similar species: This species belongs to the “Fusarium solani species complex” (O’Donnell et al. 2013) that contains numerous undescribed phylogenetic species. It has been proposed to reclassify the species as Neocosmospora species (Lombard et al. 2015). In the broad sense N, solani includes a number of species with very similar morphology, and more than 40 varieties and pathogenic forms have been described based on the pathogenicity towards different plants and mammals. Recently many have been described at species level supported by phylogenetic analyses e.g. Fusarium azukicola, F. brasiliense, F. crassistipitatum, F. cuneirostrum,
Macromorphology: Colonies on PDA at 25 °C reach a diameter of 25–50 mm after 4 days. Aerial mycelium sparse or dense and floccose, sometimes leathery, greyish-white, cream to buff, conidial slime formed in sporodochia or pionnotes. Agar surface sometimes green to bluish-brown. Reverse often in greenish or brownish shades. Colonies on YES at 25 °C have a diameter of 20–55 mm after 4 days with velvety dense mycelium often in dark rose to brownish-red colours. Some strains have a yellowish shade. The reverse is bright yellow with a red to brownish-red tinge.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph has been observed and may occur in some strains.
Chemical markers: Cyclosporine A, fusaric acid, napht- hoquinone pigments, nectriafurone.
Habitats and distribution: Neocosmospora solani is common world-wide in food and indoor environments. Occurring in soils and on a wide range of plants and animals.
Physiology: Some isolates can grow at 37 °C.
Biotechnological applications: Strains have been found to degrade many organic pollutants and pesticides. Production of enzymes, e.g. cutinases, has been investigated.
Biodeterioration and pathology: Causes root and stem rot and spoilage of many different plants. Often found in wounds and damaged organisms as secondary infections. Some strains are pathogenic to humans and animals and can cause keratitis in man.

Species description: Neurospora sitophila Shear & Dodge
Micromorphology: Conidiogenous hyphae are more or less ascending, smooth-walled, septate, with lateral branches, which form chains of conidia. Conidia are one- celled, produced in chains and connected by a narrow hyaline strand. Conidia become separated quickly and are dispersed as a powdery mass under dry conditions. They are ellipsoidal, more or less cylindrical or globose to subglobose and often also irregular in shape and size, (7–)10–15 × 5–10(–11)µm. Conidia are hyaline, pinkish to orange in mass and have smooth walls.
Macromorphology: Colonies are growing fast on most media, attaining a diameter of 25 mm in one day at 24 °C. Colonies are floccose with irregular tufts, especially at the margin of the Petri-dish, initially colourless, becoming pinkish to orange. Mycelium, conidiogenous hyphae and conidia often grow out of the Petri-dish and are able to lift the lid. Because of the explosive growth of this fungus, spoilage of products can occur within a few days.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, holoblastic acropetal and thallic conidiogenesis; sexual morph may occur in culture.
Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. Neurospora sitophila is reported from Europe, USA, Japan, Surinam and Indonesia. Neurospora sitophila is also known as the “red bread mould”, occurring on bread and related products, silage, meat, sometimes in connection with harvest, transportation and storage rot of fruit (e.g. apples, strawberries, raspberries). This fungus is able to grow into slants or Petri dishes of other cultures so that contamination in the laboratory and hospitals easily can occur. Sometimes it is also occurring as a contaminant in indoor environments.
Physiology: Neurospora sitophila has good growth between 25–35 °C and is capable of grow at a water activity of 0.88–0.90. Neurospora sitophila is capable of spoiling mycologial media stored at 2 °C.
Biotechnological applications: Neurospora sitophila is used for the production of oncom merah, a fermented food product made from peanut press cake in Indonesia.

Species description: Oidiodendron griseum Robak
Micromorphology: Conidiophores erect, pigmented, up to 100 µm long and 1.5–2.0 µm wide, apically branched. Branches, consisting of chains of arthroconidia. The arthroconidiamayalsobeproducedfromundifferentiated hyphae. Between the arthroconidia which are produced basipetally often empty cells are present. Arthroconidia pale grey-green in mass, smooth-walled or nearly so, 2.0–3.5 × 1.5–2.0 µm, ovoid to short cylindrical.
Macromorphology: Colonies are slow-growing reaching about up to 15 mm in 14 days on most media. They are greyish to olivaceous brown, velvety often with tufts towards the central part of the colonies. Reverse dark brown.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, holoblastic acropetal conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Habitats and distribution: Indoor. Isolated from soils in forests in Scandinavia, Britain, France, Africa, New Zealand, North America and Canada, Trinidad. Also from humus, garden compost, decaying wood, pine lit- ter, cedar and peat bogs, hay. Frequently isolated from paper, archives, and timber.
Physiology: Good growth and sporulation at 25–30 °C.

Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.
Species description: Parengyodontium album (Limber) C.C. Tsang et al.
Molecular markers: Three potential cryptic species within the Parengyodontium album species complex are revealed. The ITS and BenA sequences of the type of P. album (CBS 504.83) are given: ITS: LC092880; ?-tubulin: LC092918.
Micromorphology: Submerged hyphae and hyphae of the aerial mycelium hyaline, smooth–walled, 1–2.5 µm wide. Fertile hyphae mostly slightly differentiated, 2–4 µm wide, ascendent to procumbent, somewhat stiff, apically dichotomously branched, bearing conidiogenous cells in whorls of 1–3 at wide, often right angles; conidiogenous cells occasionally scattered or with two on a lateral stalk cell which is cylindrical, 6–12 × 2–3 µm, or rarely swollen up to 5 µm. Conidiogenous cells consisting of an elongate to subcylindrical tapering basal part, (7–)10–24(–30) × 1.5–2.5 µm, sometimes slightly swollen up to 3.5 µm, and a well developed rachis, up to 3 5 µm long and rather constantly 1 µm wide, geniculate, denticulate, denticles as wide as the rachis and up to 1 µm long. Conidia hyaline, smooth, globose to subglobose, sometimes with an apiculate base, (1.5–)2–3(–3.5) × (1.5–)2–2.5(–3) µm. No chlamydospores were observed.
Macromorphology: Colonies attaining a diameter of 14–16 mm in 8 days on MEA, appearing lanose to floccose, up to 2 mm high, sometimes zonate, purely hyaline. Reverse ochraceous buff or uncoloured.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, holoblastic, sympodi- al, denticulate conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Habitats and distribution: Indoor. This species has a worldwide distribution and has been isolated from air, humid frescos, water damaged and moist walls in buildings, caves and crawlspaces. Often found on dead insects in cellars.
Biodeterioration and pathology: This species has long been utilized for the mass production of proteinase K. Parengyodontium album is a opportunistic human pathogen (Tsang et al. 2016).
References: de Hoog et al. (2000), Tsang et al. (2016)

Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.
Species description: Pleurostoma richardsiae (Nannf.) Réblová & Jaklitsch
Micromorphology: Phialides arising singly or in sparsely branching divergent conidiophores. Pleurostoma richardsiae produces two very distinct types of conidia: brown, (sub)globose conidia, 2.5–3.5 µm; and hyaline, ellipsoidal conidia, 2–6 × 1.0–3.0. Phialides of P. richardsiae are 10–35 µm long with prominently flaring collarettes, particularly those producing the pigmented conidia.
Macromorphology: Colonies reaching 20–30 mm in diameter in 10 days at 20 °C on MEA, floccose, or woolly. Colony surface on MEA olive-brown, in reverse a darker shade of olive-brown.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Habitats and distribution: Wordwide distribution. It has been reported from margarine, CIP tanks, soil and wood.
Physiology: Minimum temperature for growth is below 10 °C, optimum 30 °C and maximum 35 °C.
Biodeterioration and pathology: Pleurostomophora richardsiae can also infect humans, usually through traumatic implantation, and also cause subcutaneous phaeo-hyphomycotic cysts.

Literature: Samson et al. (2019). Food and Indoor Fungi. Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series: 2, second edition. (2 ed.) (Westerdijk Laboratory Manual series). Westerdijk Fungal Biodiversity Institute.
Species description: Pseudogymnoascus pannorum (Link) Minnis & D.L. Lindner
Micromorphology: Alternate arthroconidia produ- ced from fertile hyaline hyphae, in short chains of 2–4, in terminal or lateral position, barrel-shaped, obovoid, cuneiform, often with a truncate base, 3–6 × 2–4 µm subhyaline, initially thin- and smooth-walled, becoming rough-walled and thicker walled with age. Intercalary conidia, barrel-shaped, 3–6 × 2–5 µm, smooth-walled at first, later rough-walled.
Macromorphology: Colonies slow growing, initially white becoming greyish, buff or brownish with age, velvety often tufted. Reverse creamish, yellowish with a reddish brown center.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, holoblastic, acropetal conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Habitats and distribution: Indoor. This species has a preference for temperate regions. Pseudogymnoascus pannorum has been isolated from wood, leaves, compost, archives and soils (especially Arctic permafrost soils).
Physiology: The optimum temperature for this species is 18 °C and the maximum 25–30 °C. Strains of Pseudo- gymnoascus pannorum have been reported to show some growth below 0 °C. Furthermore, P. pannorum is a xero- philic species and is able to grow at a water activity of 0.89.
Biodeterioration and pathology: This species has been implicated in the biodeterioration of antique and optical glass, which might lead to etching. Furthermore, it has been reported as an agent of superficial infection of skin and nails in humans.

Species description: Purpureocillium lilacinum (Thom) Luangsa-ard et al.
Molecular markers: Elongation factor 1-alpha: FR734156; ?-tubulin: JQ965114; ITS: FR734101.
Micromorphology: Conidiophores arising from submerged hyphae 4–6 mm in length, occasionally forming loose synnemata up to 2 mm high; stalks with roughened thick walls, 3–4 mm wide consisting of verticillate branches with whorls of two to four phialides. Phialides 6–9 × 2.5–3 µm, having a swollen basal portion tapering into a short distinct neck about 1 mm wide. Conidia in divergent chains, ellipsoidal to fusiform, smooth-walled to slightly roughened, hyaline, purple en masse, 2–3 × 2–4 µm.
Similar species: Purpureocillium lilacinum was previously classified in the genus Paecilomyces based on the production of paecilomyces-type phialides.
Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA moderately to fast growing and attaining a diameter of 25–35 mm after 7 days at 25 °C, consisting of a basal felt with or without floccose aerial overgrowth, sometimes strongly floccose, white at first, becoming vinaceous; reverse mostly in shades of purple or sometimes uncoloured.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal phialidic conidiogenesis; sexual morph not known.
Habitats and distribution: Wordwide; isolated from wet environments including water from water tanks, bottled water, sinks, showers (including drains) and toi- lets. This species can thrive on wet and moist surfaces of water distribution systems and form a biofilm, together with other species such as Aspergillus, Fusarium and Sa- rocladium. Purpureocillium lilacinum is also isolated from other substrates, such as decaying vegetation, insects, nematodes, wood (pulp), man and other vertebrates.
Physiology: No or very slow growth at 37 °C (0–10(–20) mm).
Biotechnological applications: Purpureocillium lilaci- num is used for the control of nematode pests.
Biodeterioration and pathology: This species is occasionally associated with human infections (most frequent manifestation is keratitis, but other sites of the body can be affected).

Species description: Rhizomucor miehei (Cooney & Emerson) Schipper
Micromorphology: Stolons up to 9 µm in diameter with roughened walls; rhizoids weakly developed; sporangiophores sympodially branched, up to 7 µm in diameter, with slightly encrusted, brownish walls; sporangia grey, glittering, up to 50(–60) µm in diameter, with encrusted walls which rupture at maturity; columellae obovoid to slightly pyriform, up to 28 × 25 µm, rarely larger, brownish to mouse grey, with small protrusions; collars poorly defined to none; sporangiospores subglobose, a few ellipsoidal, 3–4 µm in diameter, rarely larger; zygospores (homothallic) formed in the aerial mycelium, globose to slightly compressed, up to 50 µm, but mostly approx. 35 µm in diameter reddish brown when young becoming blackish brown.
Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA growing attaining a diameter of 30–70 mm after 7 days at 25 °C. Growth at 37 °C faster, covering the Petri-dish in one week. Colonies 1 mm in height, grayish coloured.
Habitats and distribution: Cosmopolitan, isolated from soil, compost and stored barley. This species is thermophilic and therefore occurs in warmer environments. Rhizomucor is significant for foods in (sub)tropical regions.
Physiology: This species is thermophilic and has an optimum growth temperature between 42 and 45 °C. Minimum and maximum temperatures are 21 and 62 °C, respectively.
Biotechnological applications: Used for the production of proteolytic and lipase enzymes; production of milk- coagulating enzymes for milk clotting in the cheese production.

Species description: Rhizopus oligosporus Saito
Micromorphology: Sporangiophores solitary or in groups of up to 4(–6), arising as subhyaline to brownish hyphae opposite very short rhizoids, smooth or slightly rough-walled, up to 1000 µm long and 10–18 µm in diameter. Sporangia globose, brownish-black at maturity, (50–)100–180 µm in diam. Columella globose to subglobose with funnel-shaped apophysis. Sporangiospores irregularly shaped, globose, ellipsoidal, 7–10(–24) µm in length, brownish in mass, single, subhyaline, smooth-walled. Chlamydospores abundant, single or in short chains, colourless, with granular contents, occurring in hyphae, sporangiophores and sporangia, globose, ellipsoidal, cylindrical, (7–)12–45 × 7–35 µm.
Similar species: Rhizopus oligosporus is considered to be the domesticated form of R. microsporus.This species has typical shorter sporangiophores and smaller ornamented spores. Spores of R. oligospores are irregularly shaped, large (7–24 µm) and smooth-walled. Rhizopus oligosporus is used for the fermentation of soybeans e.g. tempe.
Macromorphology: Colonies fast growing, covering the Petri dish within one week. Colony pale brownish- grey, up to 1 mm high.
Habitats and distribution: Food. Known from Japan, China, and Indonesia; isolated from tempe.
Physiology: Optimum between 30–35 °C; minimum at 12 °C and maximum around 42 °C.
Biotechnological applications: Rhizopus oligosporus is used in food fermentations, especially for the production of tempe.

Species description: Rhizopus oryzae Went & Prinsen Geerlings
Micromorphology: Stolons smooth or slightly rough, almost colourless to yellowish-brown. Rhizoids brownish, opposite the sporangiophores that also can arise directly from stolons without rhizoids. Sporangiophores solitary or in groups of up to 5, sometimes forked, smooth-walled, 150–2000 µm long and 6–14 µm in diam. Sporangia globose or subglobose with spinulose wall, becoming dark- brown to black-brown, 50–200 µm in diam. Columella ovoid or globose, 30–120 µm in diameter, smooth- or slightly rough-walled. Sporangiospores globose, ovoid or irregularly shaped, often polygonal, striate, 4–10 µm long. Chlamydospores globose, 10–35 µm in diam, ellipsoidal or cylindrical, 8–13 × 16–24 µm in diameter.
Macromorphology: Colony white becoming brownish- grey with age, about 10 mm high.
Habitats and distribution: Food. Worldwide distribu- tion, though mainly in tropical and subtropical zones. Isolated from soils, grains, groundnuts, polluted water, vegetables, decaying fruit.
Physiology: Optimum at 30–35 °C; minimum 5–7 °C and maximum 44(–49) °C.
Biotechnological applications: Rhizopus oryzae and
Biodeterioration and pathology: This species is associated with Rhizopus rot of fruits. Furthermore, it is an important agent of human mucormycosis.

Species description: Rhizopus stolonifer (Ehrenb.) Vuill.
Micromorphology: Sporangiophores 1.5–3(–4) mm tall, solitary or in groups of 2–7 (usually 3–4) from the almost colourless to dark-brown, smooth or slightly rough-walled stolons opposite the branched rhizoids. Sporangia globose to subglobose, (50–)150–360 µm in diam, blackish-brown at maturity. Columella globose, subglobose, ovoid (40–) 70–160(–250) µm in diam. Sporangiospores irregular in shape often polygonal or ovoid, globose, elliptical, striate, (4–)7–15 × 6–8(–12) µm. Chlamydospores absent in stolons, sometimes present in submerged hyphae. Heterothallic. Zygospores brownish-black, warted, with unequal suspensors, (75–)150–200 µm in diam.
Similar species: Rhizopus stolonifer can be distinguished from R. oryzae and R. oligosporus by its inability to grow at 37 °C.
Macromorphology: Colony whitish becoming greyish- brown due to brownish sporangiophores and brown- black sporangia, often over 20 mm high. Mycelium, sporangiophores and spores can grow outside the Petri dish and therefore contamination of the laboratory can easily occur.
Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor (commonly air-borne). Worldwide distribution but more often occurring in warmer zones. Isolated from soil, grain, vegetables, fruit and nuts.
Physiology: The optimum temperature is 25–26 °C, minimum about 5 °C and maximum 32–33 °C.
Biodeterioration and pathology: Rhizopus rot of various fruits, such as strawberries, peaches, avocados etc., is mostly caused by R. stolonifer.

Species description: Saccharomycopsis fibuligera (Lindner) Klöcker
Micromorphology: Abundant production of true hyphae with varying numbers of blastoconidia, as well as some pseudohyphae. Conidia arise on denticles (small projections) along the length of undifferentiated hyphae, yeast-like, spherical, ellipsoidal or pyriform, 2–6 µm long, with thin smooth walls. Budding cells are ovoid to elongate, 2–5 × 3–12.5 µm, sometimes tapered. Asci are, when present, spherical to ovoid and may be free, having formed from a single budded cell, or attached to the ends or sides of hyphae. Occasionally, asci arise on protuberances from two adjacent hyphal cells, but generally asci are unconjugated. Each ascus forms two to four hat-shaped ascospores that are liberated at maturity; 7–8 µm long, including the flange.
Similar species: Hyphopichia burtonii also spoils modified atmosphere packaged bread and resembles S. fibuligera in culture. Arthroconidia are produced by H. burtonii and this feature can be used to differentiate both
Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA and DG18 15– 25 mm diameter, dull and gray-white with a somewhat raised center. Tufts of hyphal outgrowths on the colony surface give a diagnostic roughness; reverse pale, off- white or very pale yellow.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, holoblastic and thallic conidiogenesis; sexual morph present, homothallic.
Habitats and distribution: Wordwide, isolated from cereals and cereal products. Saccharomycopsis fibuligera is one of the species causing chalk mold defects on modified atmosphere packaged bread. This species is also present in traditional Asian alcoholic starters for rice wine production (e.g. Daqu, Ragi, Nuruk).
Physiology: The minimum growth temperature is around 5 °C, the optimum around 26 °C and the maximum around 38 °C. Growth is possible at water activities above 0.82. Optimum growth at pH 5.
Biotechnological applications: This species is present in Asian alcoholic starters and has potential in biofuel production using biomass. It is a common spoilage orga- nism of modified atmosphere packaged bread.

Species description: Sarocladium strictum (W. Gams) Summerbell
Micromorphology: Vegetative mycelium is mostly hyaline. Phialides are awl-shaped, simple, erect, arising from the substrate mycelium or from bundled aerial hyphae (fasciculate). If compound conidiophores occur, branches are only restricted to the basal part (basitonous). Conidia are usually one-celled, hyaline or pigmented, mostly in slimy heads.
Macromorphology: Colonies on MEA are slow-growing, generally less than 20 mm in diameter in 7 days. The colonies of S. strictum are pale pink with cylindrical conidia. Colonies are very inhibited on DG18.
Morphs: Asexual morph present, basipetal, phialidic co- nidiogenesis; sexual morph not present in culture.
Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. Saro- cladium has a world-wide distribution. Most species are saprophytic and have been isolated from dead plant material and soil and some species are pathogenic to plants and humans. Sarocladium strictum has been isolated from wet or water-damaged indoor environments, e.g. bathrooms, humidifier water, wet wallpaper and woodwork.
Physiology: A coarse overview of different physiological characters for several Acremonium species can be found in Domsch et al. (2007). Sarocladium strictum is here listed under Acremonium strictum.
Biodeterioration and pathology: Several Sarocladium species are related to infections in humans and animals and are (weakly) pathogenic for plants.

Species description: Stachybotrys chlorohalonata B. Andersen & Thrane

Species description: Syncephalastrum racemosum Cohn
Micromorphology: Vegetative hyphae hyaline, branched, septa produced in old cultures to delimit reproductive structures. Main sporangiophores (with rhizoids) and their often strongly curved lateral branches each bearing a terminal vesicle, which forms merosporangia all over its surface. Vesicles brownish, globose or subglobose to ovoid; terminal vesicles 30–80 µm, lateral 10–40 µm in diam, with or without a septum. Merosporangia grey, cylindrical, 15–33 µm long and 4 µm wide, breaking up into 5–10(–18) merospores. Merosporangium wall thin and disappearing. Merospores globose or ovoid, 2.5–5(–6.5) µm in diam, usually faintly roughened, pale brown. Chlamydospore-like swellings more or less spherical, 12–13 µm in diam. Heterothallic. Zygospores (after 10 days on MEA at 20–24 °C) mainly in substrate mycelium, orange-brown, with conical projections, 50–90 µm in diam. Suspensors hyaline, smooth, subequal.
Macromorphology: Colony white becoming grey with age, growing rapidly, covering the Petri-dish within a week, about 4–5(–15) mm high.
Habitats and distribution: Food and indoor. Main distribution in tropical and subtropical regions; isolated from soil, dung and as a storage organism from grains.
Physiology: Good growth occurs between 17 and 40 °C. Most Zygomycetes require high water activities for their growth, but S. racemosum is an exception and can grow at a low water activity down to 0.84. Its capability to grow at lower water activities makes this species an important storage organism.

Extrolites: wortmannin-like, aszonalenin-like, chromanol-like, tryptoquivaline-like and tryptoquivalone-like Distinguishing features: secretes a blue pigment to the medium in 7–10 d; relatively slow growth on CYA at 25 °C
Holotype: Holotype of Neosartorya warcupii, here designated as NRRL 35723T (dried culture), isolated from soil, Finders Range, Australia. Homothallic, cleistothecia superficial, yellowish white to pale yellow, globose to subglobose, 180–350 µm in diam., surrounded by a loose covering of hyaline to yellowish white hyphae. Asci 8-spored, globose to subglobose 10–16 µm, evanescent at maturity. Ascospores lens shapedm 4.5–7 µm, with two prominent equatorial crests, convex surface smooth to microtuberculate. Mycelium composed of hyaline, branched, septate, smooth-walled hyphae. Conidial heads short, columnar. Conidiophores arising from aerial hyphae, uniseriate, stipes 100–150 × 4–6 µm; vesicles subclavate to subglobose, 12–18 µm in diam; phialides 7.5–9 x 2–3 µm, covering the upper half of vesicle. Conidia globose to subglobose, smooth, 1.8–2.5 µm. Colonies on MEA growing rapidly, 35–40 mm in 7 d at 25 °C. Colonies on CYA, 18–22 mm in 7 d at 25 °C, creamish white, sectors frequently produced. Conidial heads few in number. Reverse bluish in colour.
Morphological characteristics: Homothallica; cleistothecia superficialia, alba vel dilute lutea, globosa vel subglobosa, 200–350 μm diam, in hyphis hyalinis vel luteoalbis laxe obtextis. Asci octospori, globosi vel subglobosi, 4.5–7 μm diam, evanescentes. Ascosporae 5.5–7 μm diam, cristis angustis, aequatoriis binis, pagina convexa sublaevigata. Mycelium ex hyphis hyalinis, ramosis, septatis, laeviparietinis constans. Capitula conidialia curta, columnaria. Conidiophora ex hyphis aeriis exorientia, uniseriata, stipitibus 100–150 x 4–5 μm; vesiculae ampulliformes, 10–25 μm diam; phialides 7.5–9 x 2–3 μm, dimidium supernum vesiculae obtegentes. Conidia subglobosa vel ellipsoidea, laevia, 1.8–1.5 μm diam. Coloniae in agaro MEA in 7 dieibus et 25 °C celeriter crescentes, 35–40 mm diam, albae, capitulis conidialibus paucis. Coloniae in agaro CYA in 7 dieibus et 25 °C 20–30 mm diam, cremeoalbae, centro ab hyphis aerialibus laxe obtecto; capitula conidialia pauca; colonia reversa luteobrunnea vel atrobrunne.
Pathogenicity: not reported
